title: Streaming Reply
description: The AI reply surface in liquid glass. A glass header pill carries the assistant mark and a phase label that morphs letter by letter, text arrives token by token with a per-word fade and a tinted cursor bubble, inline code sits on neutral chips, and user prompts are signal-tinted glass bubbles. A long press lifts the message: the header pill swells into a glass card around the reply and Copy and Regenerate bud out of its bottom edge, and a stopped reply buds a signal Retry out of its header pill.

contents.content: A chat message that streams. Assistant replies sit on the ground under a glass header pill; user messages are a signal-tinted glass bubble.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Assistant replies sit on the ground under a liquid glass header pill: a 24pt ink mark, the name (`style.assistantName`) and a small uppercase phase label (THINKING, WRITING, STOPPED) that morphs letter by letter, the letters two phases share holding still, while the pill reshapes around it. User prompts are signal-tinted glass bubbles (`style.userBlock`) with dark house ink and a tucked bottom-trailing corner. Set `style.showsHeader = false` for a bare reply.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Text is split into word tokens (each word keeps its trailing whitespace), and each new word settles like ink over `fadeDuration`: its opacity eases out, so it reads almost at once, and on iOS 18 a 2pt rise trails it and comes to rest just after the word is fully inked. On iOS 18 a private `TextRenderer` draws each token this way; on iOS 17 the same opacities are written into the `AttributedString` runs, without the rise. Words that arrive together in one update ink in left to right, 24ms apart, never more than 0.12s (or 40% of `fadeDuration`) behind the stream. Only words that arrive after the view appears animate, so loaded history renders instantly.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: The reply text is not selectable: selectable text is drawn without the renderer, so words would land without their ink and the cursor would never breathe. Copy in the lifted actions takes the whole message.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Inline markdown renders in one weight: every string is semibold, strong emphasis included. Inline `code` sits on a small rounded chip, a faint wash of the text colour, so it reads on the ground and on a tinted bubble alike; set `style.code` to tint it, with dark ink on top. On iOS 17 the chip is the run's background.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: The cursor is a small tinted bubble sized from the body font's cap height, so it flows with the text and scales with Dynamic Type. On iOS 18 it holds solid while words land, like a caret while typing, and breathes slowly once the stream pauses; on iOS 17 it is solid. Streaming with no words yet shows the cursor alone on the line the thinking dots used, so the reply never collapses and regrows.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: `phase` is a value, not internal state: drive `.thinking` (block-colored dots rising in sequence, each easing out of rest and back, and a pulsing mark), `.streaming`, `.done`, `.error(message)` from your stream. New phases come in calmly and `.done` clears the label and cursor firmly. Entering `.error` turns the mark signal, shakes it once by 3pt with an error haptic, shows the message under the reply and buds a signal Retry out of the end of the header pill, joined to it by a liquid neck; it calls `onAction(.regenerate)` and melts back into the pill when the phase moves on. Without a header, Retry sits beside the message on its own glass.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Press and hold: after a short beat the message sinks a touch toward its tail, without bounce, and springs back if you let go early; at 0.35s it springs up with a rigid impact as the header pill swells into a glass card around the whole reply, and Copy and Regenerate bud out of the card's bottom edge, hanging a neck's width under it and resting apart from each other. A user's bubble lifts the same way and buds Copy alone. The room they take opens on a calm spring with only a slight give, so the messages around it move without bobbing. Copy writes to `UIPasteboard`, its glass tints sage, its glyph swaps to a check and its label morphs to Copied, and it pops with a success haptic; the message is set down 0.9s later unless you picked it up again. Tap the message to put it down: it lands with a little give while the actions melt back and the card shrinks into the pill, with no bounce. The lift's shadow is cast from the card's outline. Copy, Regenerate and Retry sink under the finger, glass and label together, and spring back.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: `Style` (`StreamingReply.Style`): `userBlock`, `cursor`, `code`, `dots`, `signal`, `ink`, `text`, `muted`, `mark`, `markInk`, `actionInk`, `success`, `assistantName`, `showsHeader`. `surface` and `actionFill` are kept for source compatibility and no longer used. `tint:` still overrides the user bubble and cursor.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Under Reduce Motion new words still fade in, together and without the rise. The cursor holds solid, the mark neither pulses nor shakes (its signal color shows the error), and the thinking dots stay in place while a ripple runs through their opacity, so thinking still shows a sign of life. The message neither sinks nor scales: the card swells and the shadow fades in for the lift, the bubbles fade in place, labels crossfade, and pressed buttons shade instead of sinking. Reduce Transparency makes every glass shape solid.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Need full incremental markdown with lists, tables, source cards and a follow-up bar? That is the Streaming Markdown screen in SwiftPieces Pro.

title: Thinking State
description: The "assistant is working" placeholder, laid out like the reply it becomes: a liquid glass header pill carrying a breathing mark and an elapsed-seconds label that morphs as it counts, over three presentations on one clock: block-colored rising dots, a sheen over reply-shaped bars, or a label whose glyphs carry the sheen. Plus a modifier that sweeps any view.

contents.content: Placeholder for a reply that has not started. Every presentation mirrors the `StreamingReply` layout (mark and label, then content) so it resolves into the real message without a layout jump.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Every presentation shares the `StreamingReply` layout: a liquid glass header pill (breathing ink mark, name and a THINKING · 3S elapsed label that counts up) and then content sized to a body line, so swapping `ThinkingState` for a `StreamingReply` lands on the same pill and does not shift anything. Set `style.showsHeader = false` for content only.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: `.dots` rises three block-colored dots (tangerine, sky, lilac by default), `.sheen` sweeps a band across reply-shaped bars, and `.text(label)` sweeps the band through the label's glyphs.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: One `TimelineView` drives the mark's breath, the dots and the sheen, so they stay phase-locked. It starts when the placeholder appears: the first pass enters from the leading edge and the dots rise from rest. `duration` sets the period of one pass.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Each pass eases the band across over the first 80% of `duration`, then rests just clear of the view before the next. The band slides whole, so it keeps its width as it enters and leaves. The mark draws in and turns on the same beat and is back to full size and upright between passes, which is the `StreamingReply` mark's pose. Each dot eases out of rest and back, as in `StreamingReply`.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Each second the count morphs: the digits it shares with the last one hold still and the new ones blur in, in tabular figures, so the pill only widens (with a little give) when the count gains a digit. THINKING · holds still.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Pass `tint` to use one color for the dots, mark and sheen.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: `.thinkingState(_:tint:)` masks a bright sweep to the view's own alpha, so it follows capsules, glyphs and text with no clipping setup. It runs the same paced 2.2-second pass, starting from the leading edge each time `isActive` turns true, and fades in and out with `isActive`. On a glass pill, put it on the label inside the glass, as the example does, so the sweep runs through the words and the glass stays clear.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: `Style` (`ThinkingState.Style`): `dots`, `bar`, `sheen`, `mark`, `markInk`, `ink`, `text`, `muted`, `assistantName`, `showsHeader`.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Every string is semibold. Under Reduce Motion nothing moves, but the placeholder still shows it is working: the band becomes an even glow that brightens and fades in place on the same beat (over the bars, through the label's glyphs, and in the modifier), the dots hold still and ripple their opacity, the mark rests full size and upright, and the elapsed seconds crossfade. Reduce Transparency makes the pill solid.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Need a live timeline of tool calls with durations and results? That is the Tool Execution Card screen in SwiftPieces Pro.

title: Thought Orb
description: A small dark glass ball with a Siri-style voice wave inside, locked to the thinking state and drawn by a Metal color shader; palettes for searching, reading and writing crossfade the colour with the kind of work. Its Pill is the status control in liquid glass: the mark rides a round glass bubble joined by a liquid neck to a capsule whose label morphs letter by letter into each new verb while the capsule reshapes around it, with indeterminate dots at its end.

contents.content: The mark next to the verb an agent is doing. Copy `ThoughtOrb.metal` alongside this file; its `thoughtOrbSiriWave` kernel compiles into your app's default Metal library.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Requires `ThoughtOrb.metal` in the same target. The `[[ stitchable ]] thoughtOrbSiriWave` function is looked up through `ShaderLibrary` at runtime. Its helpers live in the `thoughtOrbSiri` namespace, so it can share a target with other orb kernels.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: The mark has one look: thinking. Four thin sine membranes travel left to right through the equator of a dark glass ball. There are no motion states and no drag; the sphere never scales or pulses, only the wave inside it moves. The wave's clock starts as the mark appears.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Colour says what kind of work is happening. Presets: `.siri` for thinking (blue, pink, orange, red over violet), `.searching` (electric blue, aqua and mint), `.reading` (indigo, lavender and a teal glint) and `.writing` (red, amber, rose and violet). Build your own with `ThoughtOrb.Palette(bands:ground:crest:rimCool:rimWarm:)`. A change crossfades on a calm spring, so steps that change faster than the fade glide from colour to colour instead of stacking.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: `ThoughtOrb.Pill` is liquid glass: the mark rides its own round glass bubble, joined by a liquid neck to a glass capsule holding the label and the dots. They are two parts of one control, so they rest a neck's width apart and the neck holds. The shader ball sits in its bubble rather than on glass, so it is never glass on glass.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Drive it from the current step: `ThoughtOrb.Pill(step.title, palette: step.palette)` morphs the label into the new verb letter by letter, the letters both verbs share holding still while the rest blur through, as the capsule's width and the dots at its end reshape around it in the same quick beat, a 0.3s spring with a little give at the end, quick so it stays light in a toolbar. The mark's bubble stays put; only its colour follows on its slower fade, and the motion keeps thinking. `ThoughtOrb(size: 64)` works at avatar size.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: `Pill` derives type, the glass around the mark and the dots from `markSize` (0.47x label, a bubble 1.4x the mark) and scales the whole thing with Dynamic Type through `@ScaledMetric`. Every string is semibold. Each dot rises and falls on an eased curve, then rests, in a ripple from left to right that starts from rest as the dots appear. They run on the clock rather than a repeating animation so they stay in phase however long the pill is up; VoiceOver hears the whole label with "Thinking" as its value and skips the dots. On iOS 26 the glass is Liquid Glass; earlier it is a frosted material with a light rim, and Reduce Transparency makes both shapes solid.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: With an `action`, the pill is a button: its glass and what it carries sink together a touch while pressed, centered so it is safe in toolbars and scrolling content, and it plays one soft tap when the action fires.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Under Reduce Motion the wave rests on the pose it starts from, a fixed frame that holds through label and colour changes, and the light in it breathes instead: the four bands dim by a quarter and come back over 2.4s, then rest at full for 0.8s, redrawn at 30 frames a second. The glass, rim and crest stay lit and still, so even a bare `ThoughtOrb(size: 64)` reads as thinking with nothing travelling. In the pill the dots keep cycling too, since they only change opacity. The label crossfades instead of morphing, the capsule resizes on a short spring, a palette change is a short fade, and a press shades the pill instead of sinking it (darker in light mode, lighter in dark). Turning Reduce Motion off resumes the wave from its rest pose without a jump.

title: Silk
description: A slowly folding silk surface lit by a movable light and shaded from a real gradient normal in a Metal shader, in house block fabrics (the brand red among them) and an adaptive standard style, with optional device-tilt lighting. Content only, so it carries no glass.

contents.content: Flowing silk background. Copy `Silk.metal` alongside this file. The shader samples the fold height field three times to build a normal, then shades it with Blinn-Phong so the sheen sits on the folds facing the light. It is a surface for content and glass controls to sit on, so it draws no glass and no text of its own.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Requires `Silk.metal` in the same target. The shader samples the fold height field three times per pixel (centre, +x, +y) to build a real gradient normal, then shades it with Blinn-Phong, so the sheen lands on the folds facing `light` instead of being painted by height.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: `light` is a `UnitPoint` in the view's coordinates; move it to change where the highlight sits. `Style.depth` is the fold contrast and `Style.shine` the highlight tightness.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: The folds start from their rest pose when the view appears and ease up to `speed` over about a second; every new `speed` eases in the same way instead of jumping, and `speed: 0` eases the folds to a stop. Time accumulates per frame from appearance and wraps on the shader's exact period (about seven minutes at speed 1), so the fabric never pops. It renders at up to 60 fps, and only while something moves: with the folds stopped and `tiltLight` off it stops drawing new frames once the fabric and the light have come to rest.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: `tiltLight` starts a private `CMMotionManager` source at 30 Hz, relative to the attitude at start, and only while the view is on screen and the scene is active. The light glides toward each sample every frame (a 0.2 s low-pass) and eases toward ±0.6 of the view instead of stopping dead at a limit. It stops on disappear, whenever `scenePhase` leaves `.active` and when `tiltLight` turns off, and the light glides back to its resting point rather than jumping. It is a no-op in the simulator.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Reduce Motion holds the folds still: on the rest pose when it is on at appearance, or stopped at once where they are when it turns on, so the fabric never jumps. With `tiltLight` the light still follows the device, which is user-driven, not decorative.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: `Style.standard` (default) is stone with a white sheen in light and charcoal with a sand sheen in dark. `.tangerine` (the brand red, `#FF0000`), `.sky`, `.butter`, `.sage`, `.lilac` and `.sand` are solid house-block fabrics for panels and cards; put `#141414` ink on them. `.ink`, `.graphite`, `.paper` and `.indigo` still work.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: The radial fold term is centred off-screen, so no pinch point appears in the middle of the view.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Silk is a surface, not a control, so it draws no glass and no text of its own. Liquid glass controls sit on it well: the folds move behind their rims.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: The `#Preview` is the brand red block fabric alone, full bleed, with nothing on top of it.

title: Touch Grid
description: A Canvas dot grid that swells and warms into the brand red or another house block under the finger, springs back on release, and sends one dissipating ripple out from a tap. Content only, so it carries no glass.

contents.content: Interactive dot grid. Resting dots are a tonal ramp on `Style.dot` (`.primary` by default, so both color schemes work); under the finger they swell and take on `Style.highlight`, a solid house block. It is a surface for content and glass controls to sit on, so it draws no glass and no text of its own.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Everything is drawn in one `Canvas` inside a `TimelineView` that pauses when nothing is pressed, springing or rippling, so an idle grid costs nothing. A short task clears expired springs and ripples so the timeline can pause again.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: While dragging, the field sits on the finger at every frame. At touch-down its strength swells in on the library's press spring (about 90% in 90 ms, no overshoot), so the dots rise under the finger instead of appearing at full size.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: On release the field springs back on the library's expressive spring, dipping below resting size before it settles in about 0.8 s (the dots under a full press shrink to about 0.75x for a moment), and coasts on along the finger's last direction like a scroll view decelerating, eased toward half the `radius`, so a flick leaves a short wake. A quick tap lifted mid-swell carries on for a moment before it springs back. A new touch never cuts a lifted field short: it plays out where it was let go while the new one swells under the finger.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: A tap (moved under 8 pt, held under 0.3 s) emits one ripple ring that eases outward and widens as it fades; ripples are capped at three.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Lifted dots swell up to 3.2x and crossfade from the resting ink into the `style` highlight, so a fully lifted dot reads as solid block color.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: The `.selection` haptic fires at most every 120 ms and only when the finger crosses into a new grid cell, so a quick drag ticks lightly instead of buzzing.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: A touch the system cancels (a scroll taking over, an alert) lets go like a lift, so the grid never stays pressed.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Reduce Motion keeps the swell, the color and the haptic under the finger. The release settles on a short spring without dipping below rest or coasting, and a tap blooms in place, warming the dots around it for about half a second, instead of sending a ring out. `ripples: false` turns the bloom off too.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: `probe` drives the grid without a finger, for previews, hints, or onboarding. Its releases spring back in place, with no coast.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: `style:` sets the resting dot color (`.primary` by default) and the block the dots take on as they lift. `.standard` warms into the brand red, `#FF0000`; `.sky`, `.lilac`, `.sage` and `.butter` use the other blocks, and `.mono` keeps the single-tone ramp.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: The grid is a surface, not a control, so it draws no glass and no text of its own.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: The `#Preview` is the grid alone on the house ground, full bleed; touch it to swell, release to spring back, flick to see the field coast, tap for a ripple.

title: Flip Card
description: A two-sided card you flip by tap or by dragging sideways. The drag scrubs the rotation, release commits or snaps back by velocity and carries the flick into the landing, the card lifts toward you mid-turn with a layered shadow that slides off the raised edge, and each face shades as it turns edge-on. An optional liquid glass flip hint rides the card's axis, its signal dot smearing from the front slot to the back slot as the card turns, and the faces take semibold type.

contents.content: Two-sided card with tap-to-flip and drag-to-flip.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: One `DragGesture(minimumDistance: 0)` handles everything: touch-down tilts the card toward the finger and sinks it to 0.97, an 8pt sideways move turns into a scrub where the full card width equals 180°, and a lift without movement is a tap. The press arrives on a tight spring with no overshoot and lets go with a little give. Only the press is animated, so the scrub is directly under the finger from its first frame.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Release commits when `predictedEndTranslation` projects past 90° in either direction, so a flick finishes the flip and a slow drag that stops short snaps back. Either way the card carries the flick's speed into the landing, so it turns straight through instead of stalling at lift-off, then swings past the face it lands on and settles back: about 8° after a turn from rest, and 13° to 20° after a hard flick. The release speed is capped, so even the hardest flick settles within about 20° instead of slinging further past. Past a half turn the scrub meets rubber-band resistance that grows the further you pull, easing toward 30° past it without ever hitting a wall.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: While a finger turns it, the card lifts off the page even face-on: the shadow eases up as you pick it up and settles back down with the landing. Catch the card while it is still landing and it finishes that landing under your finger instead of jumping. A touch the system cancels turns the card back to the face it started on without committing.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Each face darkens with `brightness` as it turns edge-on and hides past 90°; the back is pre-rotated by -180° so it lands unmirrored. The shadow slides opposite the lifted edge and widens mid-flip.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: The angle accumulates (0, 180, 360...) so repeated flips keep rotating the same way; `isFlipped:` stays in sync in both directions. A tap, the VoiceOver action and the binding turn the card a little slower than a release, since they start from rest, and a second tap mid-turn carries straight on into the next half turn.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: A light impact fires on touch-down and a soft impact as the visible face changes. Reduce Motion replaces the rotation with a crossfade that the drag still scrubs, keeps the card flat, lands without overshoot, and shades the faces on press (darker in light mode, lighter in dark) instead of tilting and sinking them. The haptics stay.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: **v2:** the card lifts 6% toward you at the edge-on point, sits on a layered shadow (a tight contact shadow plus a soft key shadow that slides off the raised edge), a soft-light band crosses each face as it turns, and the scrub rubber-bands past a half turn. Touch-down gives a light impact.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: `style:` (`FlipCard.Style`) tunes `cornerRadius`, `shadow`/`shadowOpacity` (tripled in dark mode), `lift`, `pressScale`, `pressTilt`, `shading`, and the flip hint (`hint`, `hintTint`). `onFlip:` reports each committed flip. A disabled card dims and ignores touches.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: **v2.2:** liquid glass. The faces stay yours (they are content, not chrome), and everything on them takes semibold type: the piece sets `.fontWeight(.semibold)` over both faces. `Style(hint: true)` adds the card's glass: a flip hint, a small liquid glass pill at the top centre of the card, on the axis it turns about, with a faint slot for each face and a signal dot (`hintTint`) over the face showing. The dot follows the drawn angle, so it slides under a scrub and lands on the turn's own spring, and mid-turn it smears along the pill like a drop on the move. The pill never turns with the faces: Liquid Glass can't follow a half turn in 3D (it flattens mid-flip), so it stays flat over both faces, lifts toward you with the card mid-turn and tips with a press, and the card's shadow never falls on it. On the axis it stays over the card the whole way round. Under Reduce Motion the dot slides without smearing. Off by default; keep the top centre of your faces clear for it.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Keep glass off the faces themselves, for the same reason: draw badges on a face as part of it. The example's "PORTUGUESE", "3 / 12" and "MEANING" badges are light chips 12pt in from the edges and 28pt tall, so their ends are concentric with the 26pt corners, level with the hint and in line with the face's text.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: The example is a vocabulary flashcard: a butter front with a large word and a sky back with the meaning, each with its light badges, and the flip hint on. The preview shows the card alone, with no surrounding UI.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: For a full card screen with number masking and controls, see the Pro Card Details screen (`payment-card`).

title: Motion Card
description: A solid color card that tilts with the device's attitude through an exponential filter, easing into its limit and leveling out when the grip changes, with a fixed-light sheen and a layered shadow that slide as it turns. Its content takes semibold type, and liquid glass chips laid on its face tilt and catch the same light. Press settles it toward flat, tips it down under the finger and sinks it with a light impact, and Core Motion stops whenever the scene is not active.

contents.content: Attitude-driven card with a fixed-light sheen, tracking shadow, and press feedback.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Core Motion roll and pitch are read at 60Hz relative to a neutral pose, so the card sits flat however the phone is held, then run through an exponential filter (15% per sample) that removes hand jitter without perceptible lag. The neutral pose starts where the phone is when updates begin and drifts toward the current pose over about ten seconds, so the card levels out again after the hand settles into a new grip.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: The tilt follows the phone linearly up to 70% of `maxAngle` (about 25° of rotation), then meets rubber-band resistance that eases it toward `maxAngle` without ever reaching it, so the card slows into its limit instead of stopping dead. Nothing on the sensor path is animated, so the card stays with the hand.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Motion starts on appear and whenever `scenePhase` becomes `.active` while the card is on screen, and stops on disappear and in any other phase, so the sensors never run in the background or behind a pushed screen or another tab. They also stop when Reduce Motion turns on and start again, from flat, when it turns off. In the simulator the card is static with a fixed light.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Pass `attitude:` (-1...1 per axis) to drive the tilt yourself for previews, tests, or the simulator; it replaces device motion entirely.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Touch-down sinks the card to `pressScale` toward the finger, settles the tilt halfway to flat, tips the card down under the finger by up to 0.3 of `maxAngle` at an edge (3° by default) and tightens the shadow. The sheen and the shadow follow that lean like any other tilt. The press arrives on a tight spring with no overshoot and one light impact per touch-down, and lets go with a little give from the same lean.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: A lift within 10pt runs `action` if one is set. Slide further and the card lets go on the quicker snap spring, with far less give than a lift, so it never lingers in a press that would not count; come back within 10pt and it presses again, without a second haptic. A touch the system cancels (a scroll or an alert taking over) lets go the same way.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Reduce Motion keeps the card flat: no device tilt, sink or lean. A press darkens the card slightly (lightens it in dark mode) and tightens its shadow instead, and lets go without overshoot. The haptic stays.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: The motion source is a nested `@Observable` class marked `fileprivate`, because the macro's generated extension cannot see a `private` nested type.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: **v2:** the card draws a solid block (`style.fill`, red by default) with dark ink, a soft-light sheen plus a faint far-side shade whose center moves opposite the tilt, as a reflection of a fixed light would, and a two-layer shadow that slides the same way and widens with the tilt. Pressing settles the tilt halfway to flat, tightens the shadow, and scales to `pressScale`. Disabled cards desaturate.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: `style:` (`MotionCard.Style`) sets `fill`, `foreground`, `sheen`, `shadowOpacity`, and `pressScale`; `cornerRadius` now defaults to 26.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: **v2.2:** `notchRadius` and `notchPosition` cut half-circle notches from both side edges, as on a ticket's tear line. They are real holes in the card: the page shows through, the sheen stops at their edge, the shadow follows them and they take no touches. `notchRadius: 0`, the default, cuts none.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: **v2.3:** liquid glass. The card itself stays a solid block (it is content, not chrome), and everything you lay on it takes semibold type: the piece sets `.fontWeight(.semibold)` on its content. Caption chips on the card's face read as light liquid glass, as the example's "ADMIT ONE" and ticket number do: small capsules 12pt in from the edges and 28pt tall, so their ends are concentric with the 26pt corners. They tilt with the card (glass follows its small tilt cleanly), catch the same fixed light as its sheen, and keep the ticket's dark ink in either appearance. The card's shadow is cast from its outline alone, so glass on its face never takes that shadow as a dark halo. On iOS 26 they are Liquid Glass; before that a frosted material with a light rim, and a solid fill under Reduce Transparency.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: The example is a film ticket with glass caption chips, semibold seat numerals and a dashed tear line between two 11pt notches at 64% of its height. The simulator has no attitude, so it drifts through a few poses on its own.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: For a full card screen, see the Pro Card Details screen (`payment-card`).

title: Parallax Card
description: An image card whose picture drifts slower than the scroll while a liquid glass caption panel drifts slower still, so the card reads in layers. The trailing glyph is a glass bubble joined to the panel by a liquid neck; a press lifts the card with a deeper shadow and the bubble leans toward its arrow, thinning the neck. The caption is composed from eyebrow, title, metadata, and trailing glyph slots.

contents.content: Image card with two-layer scroll parallax, press-to-lift, and a slotted liquid glass caption. The caption is a glass panel inset over the bottom of the picture, and the trailing glyph a round glass bubble resting joined to it, so a liquid neck holds the two together as one surface.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: The drift is computed with `visualEffect` from `proxy.frame(in: .scrollView)`, so the card works inside any `ScrollView` or `List` without a named coordinate space. Outside a scroll view it renders static.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Three layers move at different rates: the image at `parallax`, the caption at a third of that, and the scrim scales from 1.3x tall at the viewport center to 0.9x at the edges, so the bottom reads tighter as the card leaves. The scrim follows the square of the card's position, so it eases through the center instead of turning there. All three are pure functions of the scroll position, with no animation, so they never lag the scroll.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: The image is oversized by `height * parallax` on each side and clipped, so no background shows at the extremes.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: The caption is liquid glass: an inset panel with corners concentric to the card's, and the trailing glyph on a round glass bubble that rests joined to the panel, so a liquid neck holds the two together as one surface. On iOS 26 it is Liquid Glass; before that a frosted material with a light rim, and a solid fill under Reduce Transparency. Text and glyph on the neutral glass follow the appearance: dark ink in light mode, near white in dark. The card's shadow is cast from its outline alone, so the glass never takes it as a dark halo over the picture.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Pass `action:` to make the card a `Button`; the press lifts it to 1.02 rather than sinking it and deepens the shadow, arriving on a tight spring with no overshoot under the finger and settling back with a little give. The trailing bubble leans 2pt toward its arrow a beat after the card lifts, on a slightly looser spring, so the neck to the panel thins as if the arrow were pulling it out, and it returns a beat behind the card. It is a plain `Button`, so the standard scroll delay and cancellation apply, and a scroll that takes over the touch settles the card the same way. No haptics. Without an action it keeps a resting shadow.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: The caption is slots: `eyebrow` (uppercased, tracked), `title`, `metadata` (dot-separated row), and `trailingSymbol` (on the glass bubble). All text is semibold; size and opacity set the hierarchy.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Reduce Motion disables the drift, the scrim scaling and the bubble's lean; the composition is unchanged. A press keeps the card its size: the shadow still deepens, and the card darkens slightly (lightens in dark mode, where a shadow barely shows), then lets go without overshoot.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: `ParallaxCard.Style.scrim` puts white text straight over the tightening scrim, for busy photos that should stay edge to edge; its trailing bubble is dark glass so the white arrow reads.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: `style:` (`ParallaxCard.Style`) sets `caption`, `captionFill`, `captionInk`, and `shadowOpacity`; `cornerRadius` defaults to 26. `captionFill` is now the panel's glass tint: `.clear`, the default, keeps it neutral. Tint it only when the colour means something, and set `captionInk` to an ink that reads on it. The press state reaches the caption through the environment, so VoiceOver still reads the button label.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: **v2.2:** the solid caption block became a liquid glass panel, and the trailing glyph's ink circle a glass bubble joined to it. `captionFill` now defaults to neutral glass and `captionInk` to ink that follows the appearance.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: The example renders each picture as a flat composition (a color ground, a disc, a cropped giant word) with `ImageRenderer`; no photos ship with the piece.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: For an expanding card on a full discover screen, see the Pro Discover screen (`hero-expand`).

title: Swipe Deck
description: A gesture-driven card stack: the top card follows the finger and swings from where you grabbed it, a tinted liquid glass outcome badge buds in through the card's edge, leaning in from the side you head toward, and stamps at the threshold, melting back out if you return, the cards beneath rise one after another as it leaves, and release past the threshold or a flick throws it left, right, or up at the speed of your finger.

contents.content: Swipeable card stack over Identifiable data. The deck removes the top item from `items` after each throw.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: The deck is the source of truth for nothing: it removes the top item from the bound `items` array after each throw and reports the direction through `onSwipe`. Append items to keep the stack going, or watch the array run empty.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Directions use SwiftUI's `Edge` so the file stays self-contained: `.trailing` (swiped right), `.leading` (left), `.top` (up). Down is never committed: a downward drag meets rubber-band resistance and springs back.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Commit is decided from `predictedEndTranslation`, so a flick throws even from a short drag. The horizontal threshold is 40% of the width, the upward one 30% of the height. A `.selection` tick fires the moment the drag crosses either, and a solid impact fires on the throw.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: The card flies along its actual vector (drag plus velocity) for 1.6x the deck's larger dimension, leaving at its own speed on each axis, then is removed without a transition. A release short of the threshold returns home at that speed on the elastic settle spring, swinging a little past center before it rests, and a drag the system cancels (a parent scroll, a call) brings it home on the quicker snap spring. The card's speed is the finger's, except while it is pulled down against the rubber band: there it lets go at the band's slower pace, so a release still pulling down never lurches further down before it turns home.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: The cards beneath rise with the drag, the second card first and each deeper one a little later along it, from 0.95 scale and 16pt lower per step. When a card is thrown, the cards beneath finish rising on follow-through springs, each a beat after the one above, so the next card settles into place with a little give. One more card than `visibleCount` waits invisibly at the back and fades up as the top card leaves, so nothing pops in.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Rotation is 14° per card width, pivoting on the edge opposite your finger: grab the top half and it swings from its base, grab the bottom half and it swings from its top. Catch the card on its way home and it keeps its pivot until the swing has landed, so it never jumps sideways. Reduce Motion drops the rotation, returns home without overshoot and fades the card out in place instead of throwing it, then steps the stack up on a short spring without overshoot. Badges fade in and out where they rest instead of budding, and keep their size instead of swelling and stamping.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: `swipe:` is a command binding: set it to a direction to throw programmatically (from buttons, a keyboard shortcut, or a preview loop); the deck resets it to nil. VoiceOver gets "Swipe right", "Swipe left", and "Swipe up" actions on the top card.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Give the deck an explicit frame; cards are sized to fill it.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Outcome badges are tinted liquid glass. Once the top card is a fifth of the way to a threshold, the badge for that direction (Skip, Keep, Save by default) buds in through the card's edge on the liquid split spring: the card's edge hides it until it emerges, and its glyph and title blur in just after it leaves. Badges rest where they stay in view however far the card travels, even in a full-width deck: Skip and Keep at the top centre, budding in through the top edge from the side the card is heading for, and Save at the bottom centre, rising through the bottom edge the way the card is going, since the top goes off screen first. A badge swells a little toward the threshold under the finger, and stamps on with the success spring's give as the drag crosses it. Turn the card another way and it melts back out the way it came, with no bounce, its tint draining to clear glass, while the new direction's badge buds in past it; let the card come home and it melts away once the card is nearly there. A thrown card takes its badge with it, and the card that rises starts with none. The threshold tick never doubles up with a throw's impact. Cards further down sit in shade and brighten as they rise, and the top card's shadow deepens with the drag.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: `style:` (`SwipeDeck.Style`) sets the three `SwipeDeck.Badge` values (title, symbol, `fill` as the glass tint, `ink`; nil hides one), `cornerRadius` (which also clips the badges to your card's outline), `shadowOpacity`, and `emptyMessage`, a dashed slot drawn when the deck runs out. `.plain` turns badges and the slot off. VoiceOver actions use the badge titles. All text is semibold.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: **v2.2:** the solid badges that faded in over the card became tinted liquid glass that buds in through the card's edge and melts back out. Skip and Keep moved from the top corners to the top centre.

title: Commit Button
description: A liquid glass async action button driven by one idle/loading/success/error/disabled phase: the signal glass capsule draws in around its label as a glass bubble buds out of its end carrying a spinning ring; on success the ring closes on a check and both turn sage, then the bubble melts home as the label morphs to its success title; an error morphs the label to the message on butter glass, turns the bubble into a retry and shakes.

contents.content: Liquid glass async action button whose whole lifecycle is one bound `phase`. The capsule is glass, tinted for what it says: signal to act, sage once the work is done, butter on an error. While the work runs a glass bubble buds out of the capsule's end carrying the progress ring, joined to it by a liquid neck, and melts back in once the outcome has landed; on an error it stays out as the retry. The label morphs letter by letter from one message to the next.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: `phase` is a `Binding` so the button can return itself to `.idle` after the success hold (`successHold`, default 900ms); everything else is set by you: `.loading` in the action, `.success` or `.error("message")` when the work finishes.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: The button is liquid glass. Idle, it is a signal-tinted glass capsule with dark ink; pressed it sinks and the glass darkens a touch. Loading draws the capsule in around its label and buds a round glass bubble out of its end, joined to it by a liquid neck, carrying a signal arc that winds up from rest. Success lets the arc coast to rest as it closes into a ring while the capsule and the bubble turn sage, draws the check and pops it on the success haptic; then, if you pass `successTitle` ("Saved"), the bubble melts back into the capsule's end as the capsule opens to full width and the label morphs letter by letter into the title, a check beside it. Without a title the check stays in its bubble until the hold ends. An error opens the capsule back out on butter glass, morphs the label into the message, turns the bubble into a butter retry and shakes with the error haptic on the same beat. Disabled is clear glass with muted ink.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Tapping in the error state, on the label or on the retry bubble, fires the action again (VoiceOver hears "Double tap to try again"). The button ignores taps while loading or succeeding without dimming.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: `collapses: false` keeps the capsule full width while it works and makes room for the bubble at its end instead of drawing in around the label.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: `tint` and `errorTint` still work: they override the style's glass tints and switch that state's ink to white. For full control pass a `Style` with your own tints, ink, height and font. `disabledFill` no longer does anything: a disabled button is clear glass.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Motion uses the shared SwiftPieces springs: the capsule's width, tint and label change together and land with a small give, the bubble leaves on the bud's split spring and goes home with no bounce, its tint draining as it melts in, and only the mark pops. Under Reduce Motion the press darkens instead of sinking, the bubble fades in and out in place, the arc holds still and breathes in opacity while it works, labels cross-fade, and there is no pop or shake; colors, the check, the message and every haptic stay. Reduce Transparency draws the glass solid.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Need a slide-to-act confirmation with an amount and recipient? SwiftPieces Pro has the Send Money screen (`swipe-to-confirm`).

title: Elastic Button
description: A ButtonStyle that squashes toward the touch point, stretches along the drag with rubber-band resistance, deepens after a hold and springs back with as much give as the pull put in. Optional liquid glass surfaces (signal, block and clear raised glass) float on a soft lift that flattens under the finger, and the glass darkens as it is pressed.

contents.content: Squash-and-stretch press for any `Button`. Apply with `.buttonStyle(.elastic)`, or `.buttonStyle(.elastic(.signal))` to also draw the surface.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: It is a `ButtonStyle`, so it works on any `Button`: `.buttonStyle(.elastic)` adds only the motion, `.buttonStyle(.elastic(.signal))` also draws the surface, and `.elastic(squash:bounce:haptics:style:)` tunes both.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Drawn surfaces are liquid glass. `Style` presets come from the house palette: `.standard` (motion only, your label keeps its look), `.signal` (signal-tinted glass) for the one primary action, `.block(.lilac)` and the other blocks for glass tinted with that block and dark ink, `.raised` (clear glass, ink that follows the appearance) for quiet ones. Pass `fill: .clear` for clear glass of your own. `radius`, `height` (never below 44) and `padding` are adjustable.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: States: at rest a drawn surface floats on a soft lift; pressed it squashes toward the finger, the glass darkens and the lift flattens; after a 350ms hold it presses 0.03 deeper and darkens further with a soft impact; a drag past 44pt cancels the press with a soft impact; disabled surfaces turn to clear glass with muted ink instead of fading. The glass doesn't swell under the press on its own: the squash is the press.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: The touch point comes from a simultaneous zero-distance drag. The squash leans 60% of the way toward the finger and keeps that lean through the release, so the button re-expands from where it was pressed. Dragging stretches the shape along the pull and thins it across, keeping its area, with the same rubber-band resistance a scroll view has at its edge; the pull tracks the finger directly, never through an animation.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: The release springs back past rest with more give the further the press was pulled: a tap gets half of `bounce`, a press pulled to the edge all of it. With the default 0.2, a tap lands on the house elastic spring (passing rest by about 8% of the squash) and a full pull on the expressive one (about 15%), so the button is never firmer than a plain chip's release. Dragging past 44pt cancels the press, and it lets go without overshoot, so tearing off reads differently from a tap.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Reduce Motion removes the squash, lean, stretch and offset, and every release settles without overshoot. A label with no surface dims while pressed instead; drawn surfaces keep their darken and the lift flattening. Reduce Transparency draws the glass solid. Disabled buttons play no haptics.

title: Fan Stack
description: Overlapping avatars in liquid glass bubbles that melt into one shape where they overlap, then fan apart on tap or hold through necks that stretch and snap, the hidden faces budding out of the +N bubble as it melts into them. A drag scrubs across them: the avatar under the finger lifts with its neighbours rolling up after it, a glass name tag buds out of it and a haptic ticks, and releasing selects it.

contents.content: Avatar group that expands into a selectable fan of liquid glass bubbles. Collapsed, the avatars overlap and their glass melts into one shape. Fanned, they rest apart, each its own bubble, so opening pulls them apart through necks that thin and snap. Avatars past `max` wait inside the "+N" bubble and bud out of it as it melts into them.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Each avatar's face sits inset in a liquid glass bubble. Collapsed, the avatars overlap and their glass melts into one shape; the avatar above cuts a rim's width out of the face below it, so a ring of glass shows between them.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Tap toggles the fan; a 300ms hold fans it and keeps the touch live so you can scrub. The closed stack sinks under the finger on touch-down, so a hold answers before the fan opens.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Fanned, the avatars are separate choices and rest apart, each its own bubble, so opening pulls them apart through necks that thin and snap. Avatars past `max` wait inside the "+N" bubble, shrunk with their faces hidden; as the fan opens they bud out of it while the "+N" bubble travels out with the first of them and melts into it, its count blurring away. Folding reverses: the hidden avatars melt home into the "+N" bubble as it buds back out.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: While fanned, the avatar under the finger lifts with a little give (14% larger, a 4pt rise) and the avatars either side rise a little after it on looser springs, so a scrub rolls along the hand instead of hopping. Its full name buds out of it in a clear glass tag that rests a neck's width above it, joined to it, and melts back in when the finger moves on; its first name below turns to the stronger ink, and `.selection` ticks per crossing. The lift is height only, never sideways, so the avatar that looks lifted is the one a release picks.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Releasing on an avatar calls `onSelect` at once with a solid impact; the avatar drops back into the hand and the fold follows 100ms later, so the choice reads before the stack closes. Releasing a hold on empty space leaves the fan open; a tap on empty space closes it. A touch the system cancels (a scroll takes over) lets go without picking.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Initials sit on solid house blocks with dark ink, picked by a stable FNV-1a hash of the name. `Style` sets the block list, ink, the "+N" text, the captions and the tag's text. `ring`, `overflowFill` and `tagFill` no longer do anything: the cut, the "+N" bubble and the tag are glass.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Every name is in the hierarchy at all times. Opening staggers 35ms per avatar: the shown avatars spring apart on an elastic spring, the fan's signature give, firmed up so none swings into its neighbour's merge distance; the hidden ones bud out on the bud's split spring. Closing reverses, last avatar first, the shown ones on a quick spring with no overshoot and the hidden ones melting home with no bounce. Larger groups stagger tighter so the whole cascade stays within 200ms, and the frame moves halfway through it (with a small give opening, firm closing), so the layout around the stack moves with the avatars rather than ahead of them. First names arrive once their avatar has nearly landed.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Fanned, the avatars sit 26pt apart, so six at the default 44pt take about 394pt: give a big group the room, or a smaller `size`. The tag draws about 40pt above the avatars and first names 24pt below while fanned (the frame grows for the names only), so leave room above the stack. The tag is centred over its avatar, so on an end avatar a long name reaches past the stack's end by up to half its width: leave room beside the stack too.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: `images` is a parallel array; it may be shorter than `names`, and `nil` entries fall back to initials.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Haptics: a soft impact when a touch or VoiceOver fans or closes the stack, a solid impact on its own for a pick, and nothing when the `isFanned` binding moves it.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Reduce Motion removes the stagger, the pause before a pick's fold, the scaling and the lift: avatars move to their places on short eases, the hidden ones and the "+N" bubble fade in place, the pressed stack shades instead of sinking (darker in light mode, lighter in dark), the hovered avatar shows a ring, and the name tag fades in. Haptics are unchanged. Reduce Transparency draws the glass solid. VoiceOver reads the collapsed stack as one element ("Priya Raman, Jonas Weber, and 3 more", double tap to expand) and each avatar as its own button once fanned.

title: Hold To Confirm
description: A press-and-hold liquid glass capsule for destructive or important actions: the signal tint wells out of the leading puck while held and sweeps through the glass, passing three milestone dots with rising haptics and inverting the label under it, drains back into the puck on an early release, and on completion turns sage, morphs its label and buds a sage check bubble out of its end.

contents.content: Hold to confirm, in liquid glass. The tint sweeps through the glass from the leading puck and the label inverts as it passes; letting go or dragging off drains it back. Completing turns the capsule sage and buds a check bubble out of its end, joined to it by a liquid neck.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: The control is a clear liquid glass capsule with a tinted puck at its leading end holding the symbol. At touch-down the tint wells out of the puck to the capsule's height, then sweeps through the glass at a steady speed while held, driven by a `TimelineView`, so the edge always shows the real time left. An ink copy of the label, puck and milestone dots is cut to the fill, so all of them invert exactly under its edge.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Three milestone dots sit at 25, 50 and 75%. Each swells like a bubble with a little elastic give as the fill passes it, in step with a soft impact of rising intensity.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: At 100% the channel clicks shut: `.success`, a 2% swell and the action land on the same beat, and the action never waits for the motion. The fill turns `committedFill` (sage), and a beat later the capsule draws its end in as a sage glass check bubble buds out of it, joined by a liquid neck, while the label morphs letter by letter into `committedTitle` if you pass one ("Deleted"), or lets go if you don't. After 1.4s the check melts back into the capsule's end, the confirmed block fades out over the glass in its own color and the label morphs back.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Releasing early, dragging more than 16pt off the capsule or a touch the system cancels (a scroll taking over, an alert) cancels the hold, and a finger dragged off has to lift before it can start another. The fill carries on for an instant at the speed it was moving, then drains back to the puck without overshoot, each dot losing its ink as the edge passes back over it, and the last of the fill sinks back into the puck. Holding again mid-drain starts a fresh hold: the fill keeps sinking until the new sweep overtakes it, so it never snaps back, and the dots it still covers keep their swell.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: `Style.standard` sweeps signal for destructive actions; `Style.butter` is a calmer confirm. `tint` still works and overrides the fill with white ink. `track` no longer does anything: the capsule is clear glass. Disabled (`.disabled(true)`) desaturates the control and blocks the gesture.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Phases: `idle`, `holding`, `committed`, `cancelled`, `disabled`. `cancelled` lasts until the fill has drained, about half a second. VoiceOver reads a button with the hint "Touch and hold to confirm"; its activate action performs the action directly, and the fill sweeps full to show it.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Reduce Motion halves `duration`. It drops the press, the click swell and the dot swell, fades the fill in and out over the puck instead of welling it out, drains on a short spring, fades the check bubble in place and cross-fades the label. The fill still sweeps, the colors still change and every haptic still plays. Reduce Transparency draws the glass solid.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Want slide to act instead of hold? SwiftPieces Pro has the Send Money screen (`swipe-to-confirm`).

title: Timer Dial
description: A countdown ring you set by dragging a liquid glass knob around it like the Timer dial, with a tick per step and a heavier detent every 5s. A solid ring over a minute-tick scale, semibold display numerals, a breathing signal warning zone, a sage finish, optional glass start, pause and reset bubbles that bud out of each other, and a determinate progress mode.

contents.content: Settable countdown ring, or a determinate progress ring with the same look. The ring and its ticks are content; the knob riding the ring is a liquid glass bubble, and `style.showsControls` adds start, pause and reset as glass bubbles under the dial: reset buds out of the start bubble while there is something to reset.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: While idle or paused, dragging around the ring sets `seconds` like a kitchen timer: the angle maps to `0...maxSeconds` in `step` increments. The knob rides under your finger and the ring follows it, with no lag; the value, the digits and the lit ticks move in whole steps. Let go and the knob clicks into its detent on a short spring from rest, so it never swings past the value shown, and seats with a small pop. Touching anywhere else on the ring moves the knob straight there. Touching the dial while paused starts the countdown over from the dialed length.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: The knob is a clear liquid glass bubble riding the ring, so the ring's color shows through it. It is larger while the dial can be set, and lifts while held: a little larger again, with a deeper shadow. It drops back with an elastic give and a small pop when you let go, while the ring and the value land firm. It stays on the ring throughout, at 12 o'clock once a countdown is done or a progress ring is empty.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: The value stops at one `step` and at a full turn. Past either end the knob gives with rubber-band resistance, never more than about its own width, while the value stays at the end; let go and it springs back at the speed it was moving, on the snap spring rather than an elastic one, since the ring is the time: it passes the end back into the range by under a point when let go at rest, and by a few points at most when flicked back. Drag on more than half a turn past an end and the knob comes round to your finger, taking the value there. Crossing 12 o'clock never wraps the value from one end to the other, and touching the knob at the top of a full dial grabs it there rather than emptying the dial.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Haptics: `.selection` per step, throttled so a fast spin over 1s steps clicks instead of buzzing, and a rigid impact on every multiple of 5 and at either end. VoiceOver adjusts it with swipe up/down; those changes, a new `seconds` from your code and a new `progress` value all land on the same short spring, with no overshoot to misread, unless you animate the change yourself. Under your finger the ring and knob never animate, even inside an animated transaction of yours.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: One face throughout: the ring shows the time left against `maxSeconds`, so it winds to the set time and drains back to 12 o'clock from there. A `seconds` longer than `maxSeconds`, set from your code, is measured against itself instead, so that countdown still drains from a full ring; dialing clamps to `maxSeconds`. The look comes from `Style.standard`: a solid signal ring over a raised track, a clear glass knob, a 60-tick scale inside that brightens under the value, and semibold display numerals reading `m:ss` with the leading `0:` dimmed. `Style.sky` swaps the ring; `colors` still overrides it (several colors draw an angular gradient). `knob` no longer does anything: the knob is glass.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Timing is anchored to a start date and rendered by `TimelineView`, so the ring never drifts; a single `.task` sleeps until the finish. Toggling `isRunning` off banks the elapsed time; on resumes. After finishing, `true` restarts from `seconds`. Changing `seconds` resets.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Digits roll toward the new value, up when time is added and down as it counts, without rolling past it, and change at once under your finger. The caption (Ready, Remaining, Paused, Done) morphs letter by letter from one phase to the next.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: `Style(showsControls: true)` adds start, pause and reset under the countdown dial as liquid glass bubbles. Start is glass tinted like the ring, its glyph swapping between play and pause as it toggles `isRunning`. Reset buds out of it to rest beside it, apart, while the dial is running, paused or done, the pair keeping centred, and melts back into it once the dial is ready again; it stops the countdown and sets the dial back to `seconds`. Off by default, so a dial with your own controls looks as it did.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: At or below `warningAt` the signal ring fades in over the base ring and the digits turn signal. The dial beats once a second, up to 1.2%: each beat peaks as the digits change, with a soft impact, and the beat fades in and out instead of popping, including when you pause. Finishing springs a full sage ring in under the knob and plays `.success`.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: `TimerDial(progress:)` is the determinate mode: the same ring and knob with a percent readout (dimmed %) and no clock or dial. Turn `showsTicks` off and lower `digitSize` for small rings.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Digits scale with Dynamic Type relative to `.largeTitle` and never outgrow the ring. Reduce Motion keeps the knob tracking your finger but stops it firm at the ends, drops the lift scale and the landing pop (the shadow still deepens), lands without overshoot, fades the reset bubble in and out in place, crossfades the digits and the caption, ticks the ring once per second and skips the finish scale. In the warning zone the beat becomes a brief brightening of the ring each second, and the soft impact still plays. Reduce Transparency draws the glass solid.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Need a whole focus session with task binding and breaks? SwiftPieces Pro has the Focus screen (`focus-timer`).

title: Activity Heatmap
description: A liquid glass streak calendar for habit, fitness, study and journaling apps: weeks of days drawn in one Canvas as rounded cells in solid steps from a pale red mix up to pure red, laid out by the locale's first weekday with month labels on their week columns, a semibold streak numeral under a glass streak chip that stays alive until midnight beside the longest run and active days, a scrub that lifts the day under your finger as a tinted glass tile with a glass callout budding out of it on a liquid neck and a haptic tick per day, a glass legend chip, sideways scrolling that opens on today when the weeks outgrow the width, and VoiceOver that steps day by day or plays the weeks as an audio graph.

contents.content: A calendar heatmap of daily activity with the current streak, a scrub callout and full VoiceOver support. Columns are weeks, oldest leading and newest trailing, and rows are weekdays in the calendar's order, so Monday-first regions get Monday on top. Each day is one rounded cell: level 0 is an empty field and levels 1 to 4 are solid steps of the accent mixed into the ground, up to the pure accent. Drag sideways across the grid, or press and move, to read any day, and tap to select one; vertical swipes still scroll the screen. When the weeks outgrow the width the grid scrolls sideways and a short hold starts the reading instead. The cells are drawn in one `Canvas` and hit-tested by geometry, so a year of days stays light. The cells are content; the chrome around them is liquid glass. The streak label and the legend sit on glass chips, and a selected day lifts out of the grid as a glass tile tinted with its shade, with its callout budding out of it and resting joined to it by a liquid neck. The callout melts back into the tile when the day is let go.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Pass activity keyed by day as `[Date: Double]` or `[Date: Int]`. Each key lands on the day it falls on in the calendar's time zone, so exact timestamps work and several entries on one day add up. Zero, negative and non-finite values count as no activity. If you store days as midnight UTC, pass a calendar whose time zone is UTC.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Columns are weeks, oldest leading and newest trailing, and rows are weekdays in the calendar's order: the person's own first weekday by default, so Monday-first regions get Monday on top. Days are stepped from noon, so daylight saving changes and leap days never skip or double a cell. Month labels sit above the first week of each month, and the weekday labels mark Monday, Wednesday and Friday on whichever rows they fall.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Level 0 is the empty field. Levels 1 to 4 are solid steps of the accent mixed into the ground (pale on light, deep on dark, further apart with Increase Contrast), up to the pure accent, never transparency. `.automatic` splits the non-zero days in view into quartiles, so one huge day does not wash out the rest and the busiest day always takes the top shade. `.thresholds([1, 3, 6, 10])` sets the minimum for each level; fewer than four spread over the shades, so `.thresholds([1])` draws a done or not done habit in the full accent.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: The current streak counts back from today and stays alive until midnight while today has nothing yet. It looks back through all of your data, so a streak that began before the first visible week is counted in full; the longest streak and the active days cover the visible weeks. With `.thresholds`, the first value is what counts as active. `ActivityHeatmap.summary(of:)` returns the same figures for a widget or a reminder.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Drag sideways across the grid, or press and move, and the day under the finger is plucked up out of the still grid as a glass tile tinted with its shade, with a selection tick for each new day. It springs up with visible give, and its callout (date, value and its shade, on glass) buds out of it: born inside the day, it springs out to rest just above it (or below, near the top), joined to the day by a liquid neck that points it at its day. Both glide from day to day on a spring that never bounces or trails the finger, while the callout's text changes at once, so a fast scrub never ghosts. Let go, the callout's text blurs off and it melts back into the day, which settles onto the grid and leaves. Vertical swipes that start on the grid still scroll the screen or move a sheet. Tap a day to select it and tap it again to clear it.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: With a `selection` binding, a scrub moves the selection live and release keeps it; setting it from outside selects that day and scrolls it into view. Without a binding, a scrub shows the callout only while the finger is down, and a tap keeps it.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Cells grow to fill the width up to `Style.maximumCellSize`. When the weeks would make them smaller than `Style.minimumCellSize`, the grid scrolls sideways, opens on today and comes to rest on whole weeks; sideways swipes scroll it and a quarter-second hold starts reading instead, with a soft tap in place of the first day's tick.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Today wears a ring in the text color, and days after the end date are left out. `endDate` shows an earlier range; `nil` (the default) follows today and moves on by itself at midnight or when the time zone changes.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: The current streak's label sits on a glass chip, its flame lit in the accent while the streak is alive (lit and unlit blur across), and the legend sits on a glass chip under the grid. Every string and symbol is semibold; size sets the hierarchy.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: On first appearance the empty tiles are there at once and the shades grow into them in a wave, oldest week to newest, stopping at their tile's size so none ever reads larger; today's ring is there from the start. A whole new dataset (more than 21 days changed) grows in the same way. A day whose value changes is kicked up off its tile and settles with a little give while its neighbors stay still, and the streak numeral and figures roll to their new values. Under Reduce Motion the shades are simply there, a changed day is marked by a faint ring just inside its tile that fades instead of the pop (so it shows on today too), the lifted day sits at a smaller lift without springing and moves from day to day at once, the callout fades in and out in place instead of budding, the numerals crossfade, and a selection set from outside jumps into view instead of scrolling.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: VoiceOver reads the heatmap as one adjustable element: "Activity, last 20 weeks. Current streak 12 days. Longest 31 days. Active 86 days." Swipe up or down to move a day (the value reads "Tuesday, September 30, 45 min"), use the Previous week and Next week actions, and the escape gesture clears the selection. It also offers the days as an audio graph. With a hardware keyboard, the up and down arrows move a day and left and right move a week.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: While your data loads, apply `.redacted(reason: .placeholder)`: the grid keeps its shape in empty cells and the figures redact. With no activity in view the summary reads "No activity yet".

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Dynamic Type scales the streak, the figures and the labels; the summary stacks at large sizes and the grid labels stop growing before they crowd the rows, while cells keep their size. Right to left, the weeks run from the right, newest on the left.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: `Style` sets the accent, the ground the shades are mixed into (set it to the surface the heatmap sits on), the empty, text, secondary and callout colors, the cell radius and spacing, the smallest and largest cell, and the numeral size. `callout` tints the callout's glass (`.clear`, the default, leaves it neutral) and `calloutText` colors its text (the text color by default). Under Reduce Transparency the glass draws solid. `Style.fill(level:)` gives the same shades for your own day details. `Messages` replaces any line of built-in copy, and `valueLabel` names your unit, for example minutes formatted as a `Measurement`.

title: Live Stat
description: A liquid glass metric tile: a semibold display value that rolls with a spring and dims its decimals, a tinted delta chip, a sparkline you hold and scrub to retarget the value live while a glass flag buds out of the tile's top edge above your finger with the change from that point to the latest, a press that expands the line into a taller chart with low and high, and a tinted block variant.

contents.content: KPI tile with a rolling value, delta chip, and a scrubbable sparkline that expands on press. The tile is a liquid glass panel. While you scrub, a glass flag buds out of the panel's top edge above the point under your finger, joined to the panel by a neck, and shows the change from that point to the latest one. It rides along the edge with the finger and melts back into the panel on release.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: The tile is a liquid glass panel: neutral glass by default, tinted with the block's color for `.block(_:)`. The value is an `Animatable` text in semibold 40 pt display type with dimmed decimals. A spring with no bounce interpolates real numbers through your `format`, so a roll from rest never shows a value past the one it is heading to, and in-flight frames round to the target's own decimal places, so whole-number formats never flash a long fraction mid-roll.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: On first appearance the value counts up as the line draws on, and the dot drops onto the tip once the line has reached it.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: The tile is a weighted card: it dips about 2.5 pt per edge toward your thumb and its shadow flattens. Held for 280 ms anywhere on a tile with a line, it keeps sinking a point deeper while the hold arms, then springs back up as the dot catches the line at the point nearest your finger with a pop and a soft tap. While you scrub, a rule and the lifted dot sit on the nearest point at every frame, the value retargets with a short roll, and `.selection` ticks at each point after the first. A glass flag buds out of the panel's top edge right above the point, out of the finger's way, and rests a neck's width above it, joined by a liquid neck: it shows the change from that point to the latest one, tinted sage for a rise and red for a fall, and rides along the edge with the finger without easing after it. Release rolls back to the live value, the flag's tint drains as it melts back into the panel, and the dot grows back on the latest point with visible give. The flag reaches about 32 pt above the tile, over whatever sits there, for as long as you scrub.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: A plain tap opens the tile like a drawer: the same line grows into a 120 pt chart, with its dot and a dashed baseline at the first value riding the new scale, the baseline fading in a beat behind. The card's edge uncovers a low and high row as it opens, and closing is a little quicker. Tiles around it make room on the same spring. Moving more than 10 pt before the hold completes cancels both, so the tile can live in a scrolling grid, and a touch the system cancels lets go without expanding.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: The delta is a tinted chip with ink on the panel: sage for up, red for down. It is a fill rather than a glass shape of its own, so the tile reads as one surface. It dims while you scrub, while the flag speaks for the point. Under Increase Contrast it gains a 1 pt outline.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: `Style`: `.standard` is a neutral glass tile (its `background` is `.clear`); `.block(_:)` tints the glass with a color block and turns the value, line, and dot to ink, with the delta and a moving flag as ink pills. `tint` overrides the sparkline color. Every string and symbol is semibold; size sets the hierarchy.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Under Reduce Motion the press dims the tile and flattens its shadow without scaling or sinking, the value and line appear without the count-up and draw-on, each roll shortens to a quarter second, the dot and rule fade instead of scaling, the flag fades in and out in place above the tile instead of budding, and the drawer opens and closes in about 0.2 s with fades. Under Reduce Transparency the glass draws solid. Haptics are unchanged. VoiceOver reads label and value, double-tap expands, and swipe up or down scrubs history; swiping up past the latest point returns to the live value, which then follows new values again.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: A full dashboard screen ships in SwiftPieces Pro (`dashboard-screen`).
