title: Drag to Dismiss
description: A modifier that lets a photo, card, or sheet follow a two-axis drag, rounds and shrinks it toward the finger with progress over a styled scrim, then springs back or is tossed off along the drag vector at the speed of the flick past a distance or velocity threshold. A liquid glass close bubble drops in at the top as the drag gets going, and a "Release to close" pill buds out of it on a liquid neck the moment the drag passes the threshold, melting back in if it falls short.

contents.content: Photos-style dismiss: drag in any direction, the view rounds and shrinks toward the finger as it travels, the scrim thins, and a far enough drag or a fast flick tosses it off screen along the direction it was moving, at the finger's speed. Under Reduce Motion it fades where it is instead. The hint is liquid glass and stays put at the top of the layout frame while the view travels: a round close bubble drops in once the drag is under way, and the moment the drag arms, a pill with `style.hint` buds out of it, born inside the bubble and widening as it springs out to rest joined to it by a liquid neck. Fall back under the threshold and the pill melts home; let go and the pill melts home and the bubble lifts away.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Apply it to the full-size root of a sheet or full-screen cover, or to a card wrapped in `.frame(maxWidth: .infinity, maxHeight: .infinity)`, so the scrim covers the screen while only the content moves.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: The view tracks the finger 1:1 in both axes and shrinks toward the point you grabbed, so that point stays under the finger. Past the threshold it keeps shrinking a little against rubber-band resistance instead of stopping dead, and the moment it arms it gives another 2% on the snap spring with the rigid tick, so the threshold shows as well as it feels.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Commit happens past `threshold` points of travel or when `predictedEndTranslation` projects past twice that. The fly-off follows the release direction and travels far enough to clear the container, each axis leaving at the finger's speed on a spring with no bounce, so a flick is thrown at its own pace and a slow release still leaves unhurried. The view stays solid for most of the flight and fades over its last stretch. `onDismiss` fires once, when the fly-off is logically complete.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Let go short of the threshold and it springs home at the speed it was moving, on a spring between the snap and the elastic settle (about 4.6% overshoot). Let go at the threshold, it passes home by about 5 points before it settles, partly covered as the view springs back to full size; the elastic swing would show a full-screen view's edge. Grab it again on the way home and it picks up under the finger without a jump, and the shrink moves its pivot to the new grab point within about a tenth of a second. A touch the system cancels (a call, an alert) brings it home too and re-enables the inner scroll view.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Scroll cooperation: a scroll view inside the content keeps priority until it is at its top. On iOS 18 the modifier watches the scroll view with `onScrollGeometryChange`; on iOS 17 feed it `scrollOffset` yourself. Upward drags at the top go to the scroll view, and the scroll view is disabled for the duration of a captured drag so it cannot bounce underneath.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Bind `progress` and scale your presenter from 0.94 toward 1 with it for sheet-like depth. It stays linear and reaches 1 at the threshold.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: The hint is liquid glass and stays put at the top of the layout frame, like the scrim, while the view travels. Once the drag has gone a third of the way to the threshold, a round close bubble drops in on its own. The moment the drag arms, with the tick, a "Release to close" pill buds out of it: born inside the bubble as a small round bubble, it springs out to rest beside it on a liquid neck, widening to fit its words as it goes, and the pair stays centred. Fall back under the threshold and the pill narrows and melts home on a spring with no bounce; let go, and the pill melts home first and then the bubble lifts away. It never takes a touch.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Phases run idle, dragging, armed (a rigid tick at the threshold), returning, committing. Changes to idle, dragging, armed and returning arrive on the snap spring, so anything you bind to `phase:` swaps smoothly; committing rides the toss (the fade, under Reduce Motion). VoiceOver's escape gesture commits a downward dismiss.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Reduce Motion keeps the scale at 1, so there is no shrink and no arming give; instead the view dims slightly the moment it arms, on the same beat as the tick, a hint of the fade a release brings. It returns home on a short spring with no overshoot, and commits with a quick fade where the view is instead of flying it across the screen. The scrim, the rounding and the haptic stay, and the hint's bubble and pill fade in and out where they rest. Before iOS 26 the hint draws on a frosted material with a light rim and the pill sits beside the bubble without a neck; under Reduce Transparency it is solid.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: `style:` sets the scrim (`#141414` at 0.5 by default, `.clear` for none), the shrink at full progress and the hint's words (`hint`, "Release to close" by default). Set `hint: nil` to hide the glass hint when the presenter draws its own from `phase:`.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: The `#Preview` is the single card the modifier moves: a butter boarding pass, with the modifier's own scrim behind it and its glass hint at the top.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: For a full gallery built around this gesture, see the Pro Gallery screen.

title: Floating Dock
description: A floating liquid glass dock: every item is its own glass bubble, resting apart, and the selected one floods with the signal tint. A drag across the dock lifts each item under the finger like a key while one glass name bubble buds out above it on a liquid neck, glides with the finger and morphs its name, then melts back in as the release commits; badges are signal bubbles joined to their items, and the whole dock tucks away on scroll.

contents.content: Floating bottom dock of 4–5 items, each its own liquid glass bubble, with a tinted selection and a scrub-to-pick gesture. The items rest apart, as separate bubbles. A finger scrubbing across the dock buds a name bubble out of the item under it, joined to that item by a liquid neck, and melts it back in on release. Badges are small signal bubbles joined to their items.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Every item is its own liquid glass bubble, 48 pt across, resting apart from the next so each reads as a separate action. The selected item floods with the signal tint (or `tint`) and its symbol fills in house ink; the others are clear glass with muted symbols. Before iOS 26 the bubbles are frosted material with a light rim, and under Reduce Transparency they are solid.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Selection moves the same way whether a tap, a scrub, VoiceOver or your binding changed it: the old bubble drains as the new one floods and each symbol swaps with a blur, on a quick spring that lands with a small give. The symbol bounces once as the tint lands under it, not as it leaves the old item.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Touch and drag across the dock to pick. The finger belongs to the nearest item, so the gaps between bubbles never drop a scrub. The item under the finger rises like a key (up 5 pt, to 114%) with a little give and drops back firm when the finger moves on, so neighbours never wobble. One glass name bubble buds out of the first item and rests above it on a liquid neck; it glides from item to item with the finger while its name morphs letter by letter, and on release it narrows to a drop and melts back into the item, which the release selects. A `.selection` tick fires per item; release commits with a soft impact.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: A touch that doesn't travel presses the item: it sinks about 2.5 pt per edge (92% for a bubble) and selects it on release. A touch the system cancels lets go without selecting.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Badges are small signal bubbles joined to their items by a liquid neck, up the trailing side, with ink counts that roll with `.numericText` on a spring with no overshoot, since a count is read. A badge buds out of its item when a count arrives and melts back in when it clears. It also melts in while the name bubble is over its item, and buds back out once the name has gone. On the selected item it drains to clear glass so it reads apart from the selection. Counts over 99 show "99+".

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: `Style` sets `indicator` (the selection's tint), `selectedInk`, `inactive` and `badge`. `surface` and `usesGlass` no longer do anything, since the dock is always liquid glass; they stay so existing code compiles.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: `scrollProgress` slides the dock 120 pt down and fades it. Drive it from your scroll direction (0 while scrolling up, 1 while scrolling down): the dock tucks away quickly and firmly and comes back a little slower, landing with a slight give. Values between 0 and 1 move it directly with no animation, so a progress derived from the scroll offset tracks the scroll without lag. Above 0.5 it is also hidden from VoiceOver.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: VoiceOver sees a tab bar container whose items are buttons with selected state and badge value; double-tap selects.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Reduce Motion keeps the selection moving on a short spring with no overshoot and removes the lift, the scale and the symbol bounce. The name bubble and the badges fade in and out where they rest instead of budding, and the name bubble steps from item to item instead of gliding. A pressed item dims instead of sinking, counts cross-fade, and the tuck slides on short eases. Haptics are unchanged.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: A floating tab bar with a lens that tracks and stretches toward the finger ships in SwiftPieces Pro (`lens-tab-bar`).

title: Index Scrubber
description: An A to Z section index for long lists in any scroll view: the letters sit on a liquid glass rail on the trailing edge. Touch or drag it to jump to the section under your finger with a selection tick per new section, while a signal glass bead rides the rail under the active letter and a large letter bubble buds out of the rail beside it on a liquid neck, follows the finger, rolls its letter in the direction of travel and melts back in on release. Letters without a section are dimmed or hidden, a dotted collapse covers rails too short for every title, and there is one adjustable VoiceOver element and type-to-jump on a hardware keyboard.

contents.content: A section index rail for long sectioned lists (contacts, glossaries, countries, recipes) that works with `ScrollView`, `LazyVStack` and `List` on iOS 17 and later. Touch down or drag along the rail to jump to the section under the finger. Most apps use the `.indexScrubber(_:proxy:)` modifier on a scroll view inside a `ScrollViewReader`; use the view itself when you scroll some other way, and place it on the trailing edge yourself.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: `.indexScrubber(titles, proxy: proxy)` on a `ScrollView` or `List` inside a `ScrollViewReader` is the whole setup. Give each section an id equal to its title (`ForEach(sections, id: \.title) { Section { … } }`). Jumps scroll without animation, the section's top at `anchor` (`.top` by default), the way the system index does.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: The modifier insets the scroll view's content by the rail's width (44pt at the default text size), so rows lay out beside the rail instead of under it. With no reachable sections the rail takes no space and no touches.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Use `IndexScrubber(titles, selection: $current) { title in … }` when you scroll some other way; place it on the trailing edge yourself. `onSelect` fires once on touch down, then only when the finger reaches a new section, plus on VoiceOver and keyboard moves.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: `index: .sections` shows your titles as they are. `.alphabet` shows the current locale's index letters (A to Z and # in English, from `UILocalizedIndexedCollation`) and matches each section by its whole title, then its first character, then its first character without accents; titles starting with a digit or symbol fall under #. `.custom([...])` takes your own entries.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Entries without a section are dimmed by default and a touch on one lands on the nearest section after it (or before it at the end). `missing: .hidden` leaves them out. The letter bubble and the haptic only change when the landing section changes.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: When the rail is too short for every entry (landscape, accessibility text sizes), it shows evenly spaced entries with a dot between each, like the system index. The finger still maps proportionally along the whole column, so a dot lands on the letters it stands for and the bubble shows the real one.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: While a finger is down the rail keeps its touch-down geometry, pinned on screen, so a jump that resizes the scroll view (a large title collapsing) never moves letters under the finger. On release it moves into its new place at once, on a short spring with no overshoot that is most of the way there in about a tenth of a second.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: The letters sit on a clear liquid glass rail, always there, like the chrome of a tab bar. Touch down swells the rail a little either side of the letters, a signal glass bead buds out of the rail under the entry, and the letter bubble buds out of the rail beside it a beat behind: born as a drop inside the rail, it springs inward and opens to its full size, held to the rail by a liquid neck. While scrubbing the bead glides from entry to entry on a snap with a small give, the letter under it turning ink as it arrives, and the bubble rides a beat behind the bead, not the finger, its neck sliding along the rail. Its letter rolls in the direction of travel, blurring as it goes, without overshoot, like a counter. Scrubbing faster than about seven sections a second, or turning back, blurs the letter from old to new in place instead, so the bubble never smears.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Dragging on past either end of the column (or further out than where the finger came down, when that was in the empty rail beyond the letters), the bubble gives a little with rubber-band resistance, never as far as the next row, stretching its neck. Only the drawing goes past: the section stays the first or last, so nothing scrolls or ticks. On release the bubble narrows to a drop and melts back into the rail at its letter, its tint draining as it goes, then the bead melts in after it and the rail settles; a bubble pulled past an end draws back to its letter on the way.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: A `.selection` haptic plays on touch down and on each new section, never on dimmed entries, repeated positions or the pull past an end.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: The drag lives on the rail itself, outside the scrolling content, so it never competes with the scroll view's pan; the scroll view keeps scrolling everywhere else. A system-cancelled touch resets the rail cleanly.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: VoiceOver: the rail is one adjustable element, "Section index", whose value is the current section. Swipe up or down to step through every section (including any the rail's entries do not reach); each step scrolls. Write `selection` from your own scroll tracking so it starts from the section on screen.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Hardware keyboard: when the rail has focus, typing a letter jumps to it, arrow keys step between sections, and Home and End go to the first and last. The rail swells while focused, and each key buds the bead and the bubble out briefly before they melt home.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Dynamic Type: letters, rows and the bubble scale up to the first accessibility size, then the rail collapses entries instead of growing; the bubble shows the section at display size while scrubbing. Over a dot of a collapsed rail the bead shrinks to stand for the dot.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Right-to-left: the rail sits on the leading edge and the bubble buds out to its inner side.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Reduce Motion: the bead and the bubble fade in and out where they rest instead of budding, the rail does not swell, the letter cross-fades instead of rolling, the bead and the bubble move between entries on a short spring with no overshoot, and there is no pull past the ends. The haptic and colors are unchanged. Before iOS 26 the rail, bead and bubble are frosted material with a light rim, and under Reduce Transparency they are solid.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: `Style` sets the `label`, `dimmed`, `bubble` (the bubble's and the bead's glass tint) and `ink` colors. `track` no longer does anything, since the rail is clear glass; it stays so existing code compiles. Every letter is semibold. `.disabled(true)` dims the rail and ignores touches.

title: Stretch Header
description: A hero header for your own ScrollView and NavigationStack: a semibold display title and uppercase eyebrow over a solid block hero that stretches on overscroll, a title that shrinks toward the real navigation bar, a row of liquid glass stat pills that pins under the bar, and a solid bar that fades in.

contents.content: Hero header placed at the top of scroll content, paired with `.stretchHeaderBar(title:progress:style:)` on the scroll view.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Two parts: `StretchHeader` goes first inside your `ScrollView` content, and `.stretchHeaderBar(title:progress:style:)` goes on the `ScrollView` inside a `NavigationStack`. Share one `@State` progress between them. The modifier hides the system bar background (and, on iOS 26, the system's soft scroll edge, which would haze the top of the hero), extends the scroll view under the bar, and draws its own solid bar in the style's `surface`, fading in with progress and gaining a soft shadow instead of a hairline.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: The title is display type: semibold, tight, 40 pt and scaled with Dynamic Type, with an optional uppercase `eyebrow` above it. Overscroll stretches the hero upward from its bottom edge, which stays joined to the row below, and the title grows with the pull, quickly at first and then easing toward 12%, the way the scroll view's own edge resists. Scrolling moves the hero at 70% speed inside its own slot, so neither its drawing nor its tap area hangs over the content below, while the title lags further and shrinks, sinking behind the hero's lower edge (or the pinned row) with the eyebrow fading as it goes. The inline title rises in over the last 20% of the collapse; each fade is eased, and the solid bar turns opaque gently as the pinned row arrives. Every value is a direct function of the scroll offset with no animation on top, so the header never trails the finger and the scroll view's own deceleration and bounce drive it. States: expanded, stretching, collapsing, collapsed.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: `Style`: `.standard` puts ink on a solid block hero with no scrim; `.overImage` uses a white title over a soft scrim for photos. Both set `surface`, the house ground behind the pinned row and the bar. Copy a style and change one property to customize.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: The `subtitle` row (stats, avatar, tabs) pins under the bar once the hero has scrolled past it and draws above the content that follows. For stats, `StretchHeaderStats(["5.4 mi", "1,000 ft up", "3.5 hours"])` draws each one on its own liquid glass pill, resting apart from the next, with the row's padding built in; two or three short stats fit a phone. Anything else you pass brings its own padding.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Progress comes from `onScrollGeometryChange` on iOS 18 (fed through the modifier) and from the header's own position in the `.scrollView` coordinate space on iOS 17. `progress` itself stays linear in the offset; the bar eases its own fades from it. One soft haptic marks a deep pull.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Reduce Motion drops the hero lag, the title parallax, the title's growth on a pull and the inline title's rise, but keeps the stretch, the collapse and every fade. The title then rides up with the hero instead of sinking, and the eyebrow, the title and the inline title fade over in turn, so the hand-off to the bar still reads. The hero reads as one header element and is hidden from VoiceOver once collapsed, when the inline title takes over. The stat pills are frosted material before iOS 26 and solid under Reduce Transparency.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: A full settings screen built around a header like this ships in SwiftPieces Pro (`settings-screen`).

title: Tracking Tabs
description: Tabs on a liquid glass track over a paging ScrollView. The indicator is a signal-tinted glass capsule in the same liquid as the track, riding the pages through fractional scroll progress and swelling a little while it travels, with title ink that turns exactly under its edge, optional counts, a pressed state that sinks it with the selected title, and a selection tick each time the page changes.

contents.content: Tab bar on a liquid glass track with a scroll-linked, tinted glass indicator driving horizontally paged content. The track and the indicator are one liquid control: the indicator is a tinted glass capsule resting inside the clear glass track, in the same liquid group, and the titles sit on both.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Pages live in a horizontal `ScrollView` with `.scrollTargetBehavior(.paging)` and `containerRelativeFrame`, so each page is exactly one container wide. `selection` is synced with `scrollPosition(id:)` in both directions: a tap, or a change to `selection` from outside, lands the page on a spring with no overshoot, like native paging, so the pager never shows past its last page, and the pager fits the new page's height on that same spring, so both arrive as one move.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: The titles sit on a clear liquid glass track, and the indicator is a signal-tinted glass capsule inside it, in the same liquid. It is positioned from fractional page progress (`contentOffset.x / containerSize.width` via `onScrollGeometryChange` on iOS 18, the page row's position in the `.scrollView` space on iOS 17), interpolated between measured title frames. Under a swipe it is a pure function of the scroll, coupled to the pages like a carriage on a rod: it follows them with no lag of its own, carries a flick's deceleration and lands where they land. While it travels it swells a couple of points, staying inside the track, and it settles flat on a title. A tap that jumps several pages keeps it swollen over the titles it passes, so it only settles where it lands. Coming in from a tap or an outside change it has a little give: it carries a couple of points past its title and snaps back while the page lands flat.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Each title is drawn twice, muted and ink, each cut by the indicator's outline, so the text turns ink exactly where the glass covers it and stays muted outside it. Optional `counts` show a monospaced count after each title and roll with `.numericText`. Every title and count is semibold.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: States: resting, swiping (indicator between titles, swollen), pressed (the title sinks a couple of points; pressing the selected title sinks the indicator with it), and a `.selection` tick each time `selection` changes, from a tap or a swipe.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: `Style` sets `indicator` (its glass tint), `title`, and `selectedTitle`; `.standard` is a signal indicator with house ink on it and muted titles on the clear track. `track` no longer does anything, since the track is clear glass; it stays so existing code compiles.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Titles are buttons with selected traits and their count as the value; 44 pt tall. Under Reduce Motion a tap lands the page and the indicator on a short spring with no overshoot, the indicator keeps its size while it travels, and a pressed title shades instead of sinking (darker in light mode, lighter in dark) while the indicator stays put. The indicator and the ink still follow your swipe, and the tick still plays. Before iOS 26 the track and indicator are frosted material with a light rim, and under Reduce Transparency they are solid.

contents.content: A floating tab bar with a lens that stretches toward the finger ships in SwiftPieces Pro (`lens-tab-bar`).

title: Confirm Sheet
description: A confirmation card that presents as a height-fitted bottom sheet or, inline, as a floating card you can drag away. Its confirm and cancel actions are liquid glass capsules that split out of one shape as the card lands, the icon tile bounces, and a destructive choice plays a warning haptic. Confirming melts cancel back into confirm while its label morphs through Working to Done and its glass turns sage, then the card dismisses.

contents.content: Presents a confirmation card as a bottom sheet, or inline as an overlay in the current hierarchy.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Sheet mode measures the card and uses `.presentationDetents([.height(...)])`, so the sheet is exactly as tall as the content at the current Dynamic Type size, with `Style.surface` as its background. The system sheet keeps its own presentation and drag physics.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Inline mode floats the card at the bottom of the view it is applied to, over a dimmed backdrop. Apply it near the root so the backdrop covers the screen. The solid card slides all the way in from below the screen on a calm spring that lands with a slight give, and leaves faster and firmer than it came; the backdrop fades with it.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Drag the inline card down and it stays under your finger while the backdrop brightens; pull it up and it gives with rubber-band resistance. A rigid impact ticks once the moment a flick would commit. Let go past the line and the card leaves at the speed of your flick; short of it, it settles home at the speed you let go, with a small give from below and a livelier one from above. Grab it again while it is settling and it stops right where it is, without a jump. A drag the system interrupts, such as an incoming call, brings the card home too.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: The card stays solid; its two actions are liquid glass capsules that rest apart, in one glass group. The card presents with a single primary capsule, and as it lands the cancel capsule buds down out of it, pulling a liquid neck that thins and snaps, and settles below. Cancel keeps its place in the layout while it is inside the primary, so the card and a sheet's detent never change height.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: `confirm` is async. Tapping the primary melts cancel back up into it, and the primary disables while a spinner sharpens in and its label morphs letter by letter to Working. When `confirm` returns the spinner gives way to a check, the label morphs to Done and the glass turns sage, with a `.success` haptic. The tile follows a beat later into a sage check with a small pop, and the card leaves about half a second after that, still showing its outcome. Working and Done go through `String(localized:)`.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Destructive cards use a signal tile and signal-tinted glass for the primary, and play `.warning` as the card lands, or on the tap if you confirm before it does. Other cards use a sky tile and glass tinted with the label color. The tile symbol bounces as the card lands on every presentation. Both capsules sink slightly while pressed. All text is semibold.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: `Style` sets every color and the card radius (34pt by default). `quiet` colors only the grabber now; the cancel capsule is neutral glass.

contents.heading: notes

The haptics are unchanged.

title: Permission Sheet
description: A pre-permission sheet that previews what it brings as a fanned stack of notification banners, each a tinted app tile, a line and now, that drop in one after another and deal the next to the front while it waits. A centred title and message sit under it, the request is a signal glass capsule whose label morphs through Requesting to Allowed as the stack pops and Not now melts into it, and a denial greys the stack out, swaps the copy and routes the button to Settings. Without benefits it leads with an icon tile.

contents.content: Explains a permission, runs the real request, and reacts to the result.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: The sheet previews what the permission brings. Your `benefits` become a fanned stack of notification banners above the title: each is a solid card with its symbol on a tinted app tile (butter, sage and lilac in order by default), its line, and "now". The two behind the front banner sit a little smaller, lower and a shade darker, so their edges read as separate cards. Keep each line short, like a notification ("Design review in 30 minutes"). Without benefits the sheet leads with the icon tile instead.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Present it in a `.sheet` with `.presentationBackground(PermissionSheet.Style.standard.surface)`, sized to its content (the example measures it for a `.height` detent); it also works inline in any container. The title and message are centred under the stack. About 0.3 s in, once a sheet has settled, the banners drop in from above, the front one first and the rest 90ms apart behind it.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: While the sheet waits for an answer, the stack deals its next banner to the front every 2.6 s on the settle spring, so each benefit gets read. It stops once the request is tapped, and never runs under Reduce Motion. VoiceOver reads the whole stack as one element listing every benefit.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: `request` is your real permission call (for example `UNUserNotificationCenter.requestAuthorization`). The request is a signal glass capsule that sinks under the finger; a tap brings in a spinner and morphs its label letter by letter to Requesting until the call returns. Nothing waits on an animation: the button's action and enabled state change the moment the answer arrives.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: `true` pops the stack and plays `.success`, morphs the button to Allowed with a check on sage glass while the Not now capsule melts up into it (its place keeps its size, so the button never shifts), then calls `onGranted` about a second later so you can dismiss. Without benefits the tile turns sage with a check instead.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: A denial stays calm, with no shake: the stack greys out to half strength, which reads as notifications off, and `.warning` plays. The title and message lift away through a blur and the denied copy rises into their place, and the button morphs to Open Settings on glass the label's color and opens `UIApplication.openSettingsURLString`. Without benefits the tile turns sand with a gear.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Requesting, Allowed, Open Settings and "now" go through `String(localized:)`.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: `Style` sets the surface, labels, the icon tile's colors, the banners' tile tints (`benefitTiles`, or `[.clear]` for neutral tiles), the action color and the tile radius.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: On iOS 26 the request and Not now are Liquid Glass and melt into each other through the neck; before that they are frosted glass with a light rim, and with Reduce Transparency they are solid.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Under Reduce Motion nothing drops, blurs, bounces or pops: the banners fade in already stacked and are never dealt, the labels and the two copies crossfade in place, Not now fades where it rests, and the capsules dim while pressed instead of sinking. Haptics are unchanged.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: At accessibility text sizes the button's label is plain text that can wrap, and changes with a blur instead of the letter morph.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: **v3:** redesigned around a preview of the notifications themselves. The benefit rows became the banner stack, and the copy is centred under it. The public API is unchanged.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: For a full multi-step onboarding flow, see the Onboarding screen in SwiftPieces Pro.

title: Spotlight Tour
description: A first-run feature tour for any screen: mark controls with .spotlightAnchor and .spotlightTour dims everything else through a cutout that springs from stop to stop as a red ring draws around it, and sets a liquid glass callout with step progress below or above the target inside the safe area, its glass nub pointing at it. Skip and a red Next are a liquid glass pair that bud out of the callout on the far side from the target; on the last stop Skip melts into Next as Next morphs to Done. Taps reach the real control (which can also advance the tour), stops that aren't on screen are skipped, the cutout follows its target through scrolling, rotation and the keyboard, the tour can show itself only once, and VoiceOver, hardware keyboards and Reduce Motion stay in step.

contents.content: Walks people through the controls on a screen, one stop at a time: everything but the current stop is dimmed, a red ring draws around it, and a liquid glass callout explains it, with Skip and Next as a liquid pair. Mark each control with `.spotlightAnchor("compose")`, then apply `.spotlightTour` once, high in the hierarchy: on the `NavigationStack` or `TabView`, so the scrim covers the bars too, or on a sheet's root. Anchors anywhere inside it are found, toolbar items included. Taps inside the cutout reach the real control. Steps whose anchor is not on screen are skipped; while none is on screen, the tour waits.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Two modifiers. `.spotlightAnchor("compose")` marks a control as a stop; `.spotlightTour(isPresented:steps:)` goes once on the container that holds them, ideally the `NavigationStack` or `TabView` so the scrim covers the bars too, or a sheet's root. Each `SpotlightTour.Step` names its anchor, a title and a message, and optionally an SF Symbol, the cutout's shape (`.automatic`, `.capsule`, `.circle`, `.rectangle(cornerRadius:)`) and its padding.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Put the anchor right on the control, before modifiers that widen its frame: `.spotlightAnchor("add")` then `.frame(maxWidth: .infinity, alignment: .trailing)`, not the other way round. Anchors report their frame in window coordinates through the environment, so toolbar items, safe area insets and other hosted content work. Use one id per stop.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: While a stop shows, everything else is dimmed and a 2 pt red ring draws itself around the cutout from the top once the cutout has landed. The cutout and the ring stay as they are; the callout is liquid glass. Next springs the cutout to the next stop without overshoot, morphing between rounded rectangles, capsules and circles so its corners never wobble, and the callout trails it like a cue card, landing a beat later on a softer spring with a little give while its text dips out and back so words never smear. On a long trip the give is held to a few points, so the nub never reaches the ring. The tour irises in calmly onto the first stop with the callout following out of the target, and leaves quicker than it came. `.automatic` picks a circle for small square targets, a capsule for short wide ones and a rounded rectangle for the rest, with corners running parallel to the target's.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: The callout sits below its target when it fits, else above, else on the roomier side, always inside the safe area and clear of the keyboard, resting 16 pt in from the sides and 10 pt from the top and bottom, and at most 360 pt wide. It is a glass panel with the step's words and progress, and a glass nub that melts into the panel's edge and points at the target's centre; the nub hides when the callout had to overlap the target (very large text on a small screen).

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Skip and the red Next are a liquid pair: two glass capsules that rest apart from each other and from the panel, on the panel's far side from the target, so they never come between the two. As the callout arrives they bud out of the panel, each pulling a neck that snaps. On the last stop Skip melts into Next while Next morphs letter by letter into Done, and going back it buds out of Next again. When the callout flips to the other side of its target on the way to a stop, the pair flows round to the panel's other side. All text is semibold.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Taps inside the cutout reach the real control, UIKit bar buttons included. With `advancesOnTargetTap` (the default) the tap also moves the tour on. Taps and drags on the scrim are absorbed, so nothing underneath changes by accident, and a tap there swells the callout for a beat with a light tap. Swipe the callout toward the end of the line for Next, back toward its start to go back. It stays close to the finger at first and gets firmer the further it goes, firmer still toward a step that isn't there, then carries the flick's speed on to the next stop or springs home from it. Next and Skip sink slightly while pressed.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Steps whose anchor isn't on screen (a lazy row scrolled away, a view that isn't there yet) are skipped, and the count shows only the steps on screen. While no anchor is on screen the tour waits without dimming anything, then starts when one appears. The tour gives an anchor a moment before moving on, so toolbar items that report late and the frame changes of a rotation never make it jump. The cutout follows its target through scrolling, rotation, size changes and the keyboard.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: `isPresented` works with `@AppStorage`: `@AppStorage("inbox.showTour") var showTour = true` shows it until it is finished or skipped. Or pass `showOnceKey: "inbox.tour.v1"` and the tour presents itself the first time the view appears and records completion in `UserDefaults`; `.spotlightTour(steps, showOnceKey:)` does the same without a binding. `SpotlightTour.resetShowOnce(_:)` brings it back, for a "Show tips again" setting.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: `step:` takes an optional binding to the current step, to resume a tour or move it on when someone completes the thing you pointed at. The tour writes it as people move through and sets it back to 0 when it ends. `onFinish` reports `.completed` or `.skipped`.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: VoiceOver: while the tour shows it is modal and the screen under it is hidden; focus moves to the callout's words, which are read before Skip and Next wherever the pair sits, and read "Step 2 of 4. Find it fast. Narrow the inbox by sender, date, attachments or unread." Skip and Next are buttons, Previous step is a custom action, the escape gesture skips, and each step change is announced.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Hardware keyboard: Return is Next or Done, Escape skips, and the arrow keys move along the steps in reading order. The tour never takes focus, so a text field keeps its keyboard.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Dynamic Type: the callout grows and flips above its target when it no longer fits below. At accessibility sizes Next and Skip stack full width, the symbol tile steps aside and the callout may use the full width. RTL mirrors the callout; the cutout stays on the physical control.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Reduce Motion: the cutout, ring and callout crossfade from stop to stop instead of travelling, the ring appears without drawing, and nothing scales. Skip and Next are simply there instead of budding, Skip fades instead of melting into Next, and Next and Done crossfade. A scrim tap shades the callout for a beat instead of swelling it (darker in light mode, lighter in dark), and Next and Skip shade the same way instead of sinking.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Haptics: a selection tick when a step changes, a soft impact when the tour ends, a light tap for a nudge. Nothing when the tour appears on its own.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: All copy goes through `String(localized:)` and can be replaced with `Messages` (Next, Done, Skip, Previous step and the "2 of 4" and "Step 2 of 4" formats). `Style` sets the scrim, the accent used for the ring, the current step and the Next bubble, its ink, the callout's glass tint (`.clear`, the default, leaves it neutral) and text colors, the track, the corner radius, the ring width and the callout's widest size.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: On iOS 26 the callout, its nub and the pair are Liquid Glass in one group, so they melt into each other through the neck; before that they are frosted glass with a light rim, and with Reduce Transparency they are solid.

title: Toast
description: A single liquid glass toast. A glass card carries the message, an optional detail line; as it lands, a tile bubble tinted for its kind buds out of its leading end with a countdown ring that drains around its glyph and pauses while touched, and an action such as Undo buds out of its trailing end as a signal bubble, both joined to the card by liquid necks. Placed inside the safe area so it clears the Dynamic Island and rides above the keyboard.

contents.content: Presents one transient toast on the top or bottom edge.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Single instance by design. Presenting again while visible does nothing. Every touch, release, action and new toast starts a fresh run of the countdown, and only the latest run can dismiss, so a timer left over from an earlier toast never closes a newer one.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: The toast is liquid glass, in three parts that rest joined: a glass card with the message and the detail, a round tile bubble at its leading end, and the action bubble at its trailing end, each held to the card by a liquid neck. The tile is tinted for its kind: `.success` sage, `.warning` and `.error` butter, and `.info` clear glass. All text is semibold.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: It arrives calmly from its edge, landing with a slight give, with the message already in place, so it can be read at once. As it settles the tile buds out of the card's leading end and then the action out of its trailing end, each pulling a neck as it springs to its place, with the kind's haptic (success, warning, error, or a soft tap for info). Both bubbles keep their place in the layout while they are inside the card, so the card never resizes. It leaves faster and firmer than it came, all in one piece, and slides all the way out past its edge. The presentation animation is scoped to the toast, so changes the host makes in the same transaction keep their own animation.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: `detail` adds a quieter second line. The action is a signal bubble: tapping it swaps the title for a check, pops the bubble with a light haptic, runs the handler, then dismisses a beat later. It still dismisses if the handler takes the view away first (switching tabs, pushing a screen), so the action never comes back live.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: The countdown is a `.task` on the toast and is cancelled the moment the toast leaves. Touching the toast pauses it: the thin bar freezes and the toast sinks toward your finger. Releasing resumes from where it stopped, and so does a touch the system interrupts, such as an incoming call.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Swipe toward the edge to dismiss. The toast stays under your finger that way and gives with rubber-band resistance the other way. A swipe that would carry past 40 points leaves at the toast's own speed; anything shorter springs back at the speed you let go, with a little give past its resting place. Grabbing it again while it springs back takes it over from where it is, without a jump.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: On iOS 26 the parts are Liquid Glass and the necks between them are real; before that they are frosted glass with a light rim. With Reduce Transparency they are solid, so the toast reads the same over any content.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: With Reduce Motion the toast fades in and out, the bubbles fade in where they rest instead of budding, the press dims instead of sinking, and the action's pop is off. Haptics, the tile's tint and the check still say what happened.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Placement reads the safe area of the view it is applied to: at the top it clears the Dynamic Island, at the bottom it rises with the keyboard. Apply the modifier to a view that does not ignore safe areas.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Colors live in `Toast.Appearance` (passed as `appearance:`), because `Toast.Style` already names the kind. `surface` and `info` default to `.clear`, which leaves them neutral glass; any other color tints that glass.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: The message and detail are posted as a VoiceOver announcement on appear; the action button is a real button with its own label.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: For stacked, queued alerts with a notifications feed, see the Notifications screen (toast stack) in SwiftPieces Pro.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: **v2.3:** the countdown is a ring around the tile's glyph rather than a line under the card: it drains clockwise from the top on a faint track, holds while the toast is touched and once the action has run, and resumes with what is left. It is a clock, so it keeps running under Reduce Motion.

title: Expandable Text
description: A paragraph clamped to a line limit that measures whether it is really truncated, and only then fades the end of its last line into a small liquid glass "more" pill; tapping grows the block smoothly to its full height with no reflow while the pill rides its bottom edge down and morphs to "less", links stay tappable, and VoiceOver always reads the whole text.

contents.content: A "Read more" paragraph that shows a `more` pill only when the text is actually truncated. SwiftUI cannot tell you whether a `Text` was truncated, so this measures three hidden copies at the real width: the full text, the text at `lineLimit` lines, and the text at one line fewer (which locates the last visible line). The copies re-measure on width, Dynamic Type and text changes. When the full height exceeds the limited height, the visible text is laid out in full and clipped to the limited height; the end of the last line fades out (a transparent mask, so it works over any background) and a small glass pill reading `more` sits in the faded space on the trailing edge. Expanding animates the clip to the full height, so lines never reflow or jump, and the pill rides the text's bottom edge down to sit under it, its label morphing to `less`. The toggle runs in one transaction, so a card or row around the piece grows and shrinks with the text. Font and color come from the environment like `Text`: apply `.font(...)`, `.foregroundStyle(...)` and `.multilineTextAlignment(...)` to the piece. VoiceOver reads the full text in both states and gets "Show more" / "Show less" actions; the visual pill is hidden from it.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: SwiftUI has no API that reports truncation. The piece lays out three hidden copies at the paragraph's real width: the full text, the text at `lineLimit` lines, and the text at one line fewer. The "more" pill appears only when the full height is taller than the clamped height, so a short text never shows it.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: The copies re-measure whenever the width, Dynamic Type size, font or text changes (`onGeometryChange` on iOS 18, a `GeometryReader` on iOS 17). They never read the expanded state, so there is no layout loop.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Until the first measurement lands, a plain `lineLimit` Text shows the same first lines, so first appearance does not jump.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Collapsed, the full text is clipped to the clamped height. The end of the last line fades to transparent through a mask and the link sits in the faded space as a small liquid glass pill reading "more", centred on the line. The mask needs no background color, so it works over cards, images and materials. Set `Style.fade` to paint a gradient into a solid color instead.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Expanding animates the clip height to the full height. Lines are laid out once at full length, so nothing reflows or jumps. The text unfurls on a calm spring with no visible overshoot and tucks back a little quicker. The pill rides the text's bottom edge on the same curve: down from the last line to hang just under the text as it opens, its label morphing letter by letter from "more" to "less", and back up as it closes. The fade at the end of the last line fills back in as the pill leaves it and returns a beat into the collapse, once the fold has passed most of the lines below it. This holds whether the piece is pinned at the top, the bottom or the center. With `showsLess: false` the paragraph stays open, and the pill sinks away once it does.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: The pill is neutral glass, so it stays quiet inside reading text; its label is `Style.link`. On iOS 26 it is Liquid Glass and swells under a press; before iOS 26 it is frosted; under Reduce Transparency it is an opaque fill. The labels are localized keys, so the morph is `Text`'s own letter-by-letter content transition.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Taps on the pill, the body and the VoiceOver actions toggle inside one animation, so a card or row around the piece grows and shrinks with the text. If you drive `isExpanded` yourself, change it inside `withAnimation` and the text folds on your animation together with its container; changed without one, the paragraph still folds on its own curve but its container jumps to the new height. The faded line end keeps its own timing either way, tuned to the piece's collapse.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Font, color and alignment come from the environment, like `Text`: `.font`, `.foregroundStyle`, `.multilineTextAlignment`.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: `AttributedString` keeps bold, italics and links. With `togglesOnTap`, tapping the body toggles too; a tap that opens a link does not toggle, and lines hidden below the fold have no hit area. Links open through your `openURL` environment action.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: `isExpanded` lets you drive or observe the state, for example to keep one review open at a time.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: RTL: the fade and the pill sit on the trailing side, which is the left in right-to-left languages.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: `Style` sets the pill's label color and weight (semibold, the house weight, by default), fade width (scaled with Dynamic Type) and the optional solid fade color. `.disabled(true)` dims the pill's label and stops toggling. All of the piece's type is semibold.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Reduce Motion: the text opens in a 0.2 second ease and closes in 0.18 seconds, with no spring. The pill still moves with the bottom edge of the text and its label cross-fades; the fade waits until the collapse is landing.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: VoiceOver reads the full text in both states, with links in the rotor. "Show more" and "Show less" actions resize the paragraph for sighted VoiceOver users; the visual pill is hidden from VoiceOver.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: The pill draws at one line tall but has a hit area of at least 44 by 44 points. There are no haptics: this is reading content.

title: Glass Text
description: Liquid Glass rendered on the actual glyph outlines of a string, one or several lines, set in the house semibold by default, with a specular frosted fallback below iOS 26, a solid fill under Reduce Transparency and Dynamic Type scaling.

contents.content: Liquid Glass applied to text outlines via Core Text glyph paths. The glyph path is built from the string and font when the view's body runs, then handed to `glassEffect(_:in:)` as a shape. Its subject is glass itself, so it draws its glass directly rather than on a liquid group's shapes. Split the string with `\n` for a stacked display title; lines use tight display leading.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Glyph outlines come from Core Text (`CTFontCreatePathForGlyph`), so any `UIFont` works, including custom families. The default is the system font at the house weight, semibold, like all SwiftPieces type; the example sets its numerals at 120pt so the strokes stay wide enough to bend the light. The path is built in `body`, not on layout passes, so keep `GlassText` out of anything that re-renders every frame: put the clock on the backdrop, as the example does, and leave the glass outside it.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: On iOS 26 the outline is passed to `glassEffect(_:in:)` as a shape. Glass is this piece's subject, so it draws its glass directly instead of through the liquid group the other pieces share; the glass call needs the iOS 26 SDK and is compiled only with it, so the piece still builds with Xcode 16. Below iOS 26 the outline is filled with `.ultraThinMaterial` and a hairline highlight; Reduce Transparency fills it with `.primary` instead.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: The point size follows Dynamic Type via `@ScaledMetric(relativeTo: .largeTitle)`, capped at 1.6x so a display word never leaves the screen. Pass `scalesWithDynamicType: false` to pin it.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Glass reads best over a backdrop with soft tonal variation; a flat color gives it nothing to refract.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Split the string with `\n` for a stacked display title. `Style.alignment` and `Style.leading` (0.86 of the font's line height by default) lay out the lines.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: States: Liquid Glass on iOS 26 with a soft lift shadow; below iOS 26 a layered fallback (Material, optional tint at `fallbackTintAmount`, a top light and a 1pt specular rim); under Reduce Transparency a solid `Style.solidFill` (`.primary` by default).

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: The letters have no motion of their own: no entrance, no idle loop, no press. A new string takes the old one's place at once, so letters that did not change never dim or double up mid-swap. For numerals that tick, such as a clock, use `UIFont.monospacedDigitSystemFont(ofSize:weight:)` so unchanged digits keep their place. The life comes from the backdrop moving behind the glass.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Reduce Motion changes nothing in the component, since nothing in it moves. The example's color blocks start from a rest pose when the view appears and ease into their drift over two seconds; under Reduce Motion they hold that rest pose, and turning it off starts the drift again from rest.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: VoiceOver reads the lines as one static text.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: For a full purchase screen built around glass display type, see the Pro Purchase screen.

title: Picture Headline
description: A semibold headline with living pictures stuck between its words like a hand-placed collage. Each word rises into place and each picture opens from a dot into a tilted sticker with a white rim, landing with a spring, a light tick and a flash of crop marks, then keeps drifting. Press a sticker to lift it. Use the built-in house-palette scenes (the sun is our red mascot), your own images or SF Symbols; it wraps like text at any width and Dynamic Type size.

contents.content: A headline with pictures stuck between its words like stickers, revealed in reading order. Write it as a list of segments: strings are words, pictures sit where you put them. `swift PictureHeadline(["Slow", .art(.sun), "mornings, long", .art(.waves), "walks and early", .art(.moon), "nights."]) .font(.system(size: 40, weight: .semibold)) ` Words are set in the house weight, semibold. Pictures are sized from the font, so they follow Dynamic Type and every font you set. Each lands as a sticker: a white rim, a soft shadow and a small tilt that alternates along the headline, with crop marks flashing at its corners. Press and hold one to lift it. Text wraps word by word and a picture never breaks from the row it lands on.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Write the headline as a list: string literals are words and pictures go where you put them, for example `["Slow", .art(.sun), "mornings, long", .art(.waves), "walks."]`. A string can hold several words; each word rises on its own.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Pictures land as stickers: a white rim, a soft shadow and a small resting tilt that alternates along the headline (`Style.tilt`, 4 degrees at most), so a line reads as placed by hand. As each one lands, four hairline crop marks snap in at its corners, contracting onto them, and clear a moment later: the crosses SwiftPieces draws on its artboards. `Style.tilt = 0` lays them flat, `Style.rim = 0` drops the rim and `Style.cropMarks = false` skips the marks.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Press and hold a sticker to lift it: it peels up at once on a spring with no overshoot under the finger, straightening and scaling up with a deeper shadow above its neighbours. A light tick lands once the hold has lasted a moment, so a quick tap or a scroll that starts on a sticker stays silent. It stays up until you let go, then drops back to its tilt with a little give. The press uses `onLongPressGesture(onPressingChanged:)` with a small tolerance, so scrolling over the headline still scrolls. A hold claims the touch, so a headline inside a `Button` or a tappable card doesn't also trigger it; a quick tap still passes through. `Style.lifts = false` turns the lift off.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Words are set in the house weight, semibold, at the piece's root; size carries the hierarchy, as the example's `.font(.system(size: 40, weight: .semibold))` shows.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Pictures are sized from the font: `Style.pictureHeight` is a fraction of the line height (0.82 by default) and each picture's `width` is in picture heights (2.4 is a wide frame, 1 a square). Set the font with `.font(...)` as usual and the pictures follow it, Dynamic Type included.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Words and pictures wrap like text with a private `Layout`, so the headline breaks across rows at any width and a picture never splits from the row it lands on. `alignment` sets each row's alignment.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: The reveal runs in reading order. Each word slides up from behind its own baseline on a calm spring that never overshoots. Each picture appears as a dot as tall as the frame and widens into the full sticker on the opening spring (`Style.openDuration` and `Style.openBounce`), swelling a little past full width, picture and rim together, before it settles; its tilt lands a beat behind the frame as follow-through, and its contents settle from a slight zoom just after the frame lands. The stagger is sized from the number of items, so a short and a long headline both land in about `duration` (1.2 seconds by default). `delay` holds the start; change `trigger` to replay. The old headline fades out with the words it was showing, and the new one rises a beat behind it, so changing the segments and the trigger together (a pager, say) moves from one headline to the next without a cut.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Three kinds of picture: `.art(_:)` draws one of five built-in scenes in the house palette (`.sun` is the red SwiftPieces mascot, bobbing and blinking over the sand; `.waves`, `.moon`, `.hills` and `.bloom`), so a headline looks finished before you have artwork; `.image(_:)` fills the frame with your own `Image`; `.symbol(_:fill:ink:)` sets an SF Symbol on a solid block.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: After landing, pictures keep moving: each starts from a still rest pose as it lands and eases into its drift over about a second, each on its own clock. Scenes drift (the sun bobs and blinks, the sea slides, stars twinkle), images pan slowly and symbols bob. Set `Style.drift = false` for still pictures. Drawing uses `Canvas` driven by a `TimelineView` at up to 30 frames a second, paused until the picture lands.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: `revealOnScroll` waits until the headline scrolls into view with `onScrollVisibilityChange` on iOS 18; on iOS 17 it reveals on appear.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Haptics: a light tick as each picture's frame lands, timed from the opening spring and on the beat of its crop marks, and another when a hold lifts one. Under Reduce Motion one tick marks the moment the headline has faded in. A headline fading out for a replay never ticks. Pass `haptics: false` to stay silent.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: VoiceOver reads the headline as one header: the words in order, plus a picture's `label` where it sits, so `.art(.sun, label: "a sunrise")` is read and an unlabelled picture is skipped.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Reduce Motion keeps the feedback and drops the movement: words and pictures fade in together, and pictures sit flat and still on their rest pose (the sun with its eyes open), with no rise, zoom, tilt, crop marks or drift. A held sticker deepens its shadow and shifts its brightness slightly instead of lifting (darker in light mode, lighter in dark mode), one tick marks the landing, and a replay fades the old headline out just ahead of the new one fading in.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: `Style` (`.standard` is the house look): `pictureHeight`, `cornerRadius` (a fraction of the picture height; 0.5 makes a capsule), `tilt`, `rim`, `rimColor`, `cropMarks`, `lifts`, `drift`, `openDuration` and `openBounce`.

title: Text Reveal
description: Reveals a headline by characters, words or lines, rising from a baseline mask with a stagger sized to land in under a second, then grows a stroke of tinted liquid glass behind each phrase that matters, the text flipping to ink exactly under its edge.

contents.content: Staggered text reveal that wraps correctly at any width and Dynamic Type size. The stagger is derived from the unit count, so a 3-word title and a 60-character sentence both finish in about `duration`. Phrases listed in `highlights` get a stroke of tinted liquid glass that grows in behind them once they land, with the text flipping to the house ink under its edge.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: The stagger is computed from the unit count: each unit takes about half a second to land and the rest of `duration` is spread across the starts, so long sentences do not crawl. The starts are eased rather than even: the first units leave a little closer together and the last ones settle in with a little more room, and the total stays the same. Pass a larger `duration` for a slower reveal.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Words and characters are laid out by a private wrapping `Layout`, so the text breaks across rows like normal text and characters never split a word. `.lines` renders each `\n`-separated line as one wrapping `Text`. All motion is render-only (offset, blur, scale, a drawn path), so wrapping never shifts during a reveal.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Splitting text into `Text` views loses kerning and ligatures between units; `.words` keeps them inside each word and is the best default for body-sized type.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Every preset arrives on the same calm spring with no visible overshoot, so a word never bobs past its baseline. `.rise` slides each unit up from behind its own baseline (a mask at the unit's bottom edge); set `Style.masksRise = false` for a 10pt float instead. `.blur` resolves from `Style.blurRadius` and `.soften` scales up slightly from the baseline as it fades in.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: `highlights` takes whole-word phrases. A matched phrase is kept on one row. Once its last unit has nearly landed, a stroke of liquid glass tinted `Style.highlight` (butter by default) grows in behind it from the leading edge like a highlighter, keeping its round caps the whole way, on one smooth pass of `Style.highlightDuration` with no overshoot. An ink copy of the phrase in `Style.highlightInk` (the house ink) is uncovered by the same stroke while the base text gives way under it, so the color flips exactly under its edge. The highlights share one liquid group: two highlighted phrases side by side flow into one stroke. Under Reduce Transparency the glass is a solid block of the tint; before iOS 26 it is frosted.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Type is semibold, the house weight, set at the piece's root; size and colour carry the hierarchy.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: `revealOnScroll` uses `onScrollVisibilityChange` on iOS 18; on iOS 17 it reveals on appear. Change `trigger` to replay: the current text fades out as one piece where it stands, and once it has mostly cleared (after about 0.16 s, added to `delay`) the new reveal rises in its place. When `text` changes along with `trigger`, the old text is what fades; a new `text` without a new `trigger` swaps in place with no replay. The layout takes the new text's size at once, since a fading copy takes no space.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Reduce Motion keeps the reveal and drops the movement: every unit fades in together with no lift, blur or scale, a highlight then fades in behind its phrase at full length instead of growing across, and a replay fades the old text out, then the new one in.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: VoiceOver reads the whole string as one element from the start, whatever the reveal is doing.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: `Style` (`.standard` uses the house palette): `highlight`, `highlightInk`, `masksRise`, `blurRadius`, `highlightDuration`.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: For a complete first-run flow with revealed headlines, see the Pro Onboarding screen.
